Q-Source / Notes:
We talked about…
Keeping commitments is about one thing:
Trust.
When you keep commitments to others, you build trust with them
When you keep commitments to yourself, you build trust in yourself
And if a man doesn’t trust himself… everything else starts to wobble.

Question Becomes… where do we start if we currently aren’t there??

@D20 laid out a great plan and here are some points he put together…
 
Step 1: Find a goal in your job, your personal fitness, your home life that is realistic and attainable.

Step 2: Clear the path to your goal. Preparation is everything to help ensure success.

Step 3: Execute.

Step 4: Repeat from step 1 and find a new goal.

Step 5: You HC'ed and missed. You were going to run and woke up with a runny nose. You missed a deadline at work. Take ownership of the things you can. 

Step 6: Be kind to yourself and others. You screwed up. You're not a screw-up. Stay positive and get back up, dust yourself off, and do it again. You've got this.

Lean on your brothers, form a shield lock and realize you are not alone in this venture.

Discussion Questions:
1) Where in your life do you tend to swing too far one way: trusting only yourself, or refusing to trust yourself at all? What has that cost you?

2) How do you personally distinguish between humility and false humility? When have you downplayed something you should have owned?

3) Think of a time you prayed (or reflected), then acted decisively. What gave you the confidence to move forward without having all the answers?

4) What small promises to yourself have you kept (or broken) that have either built or damaged your self-trust?

5) If trusting a higher power and trusting yourself are not opposites, what does it look like in your life when they are working together?

6) When someone compliments you, what is your first internal reaction — and what does that reveal about your level of self-trust?

 Fact: The Texas A&M Women’s Tennis team won the 2026 NCAA National Championship, defeating Auburn 4-1 in the final. This is their second national title in three years.

Thang 1 – Championship Rotations (Cardio + Core with Cinderblocks)
Grab a cinderblock (Cindy). Complete 4 rounds at tennis court:
* 15 Block Curls – at side baseline
* 15 Block Overhead Presses – at middle area
* 15 Block Goblet Squats – at opposite baseline
* 15 BBSUs with Cindy – back at original baseline
After each round: Jog court perimeter.

Q Source: Self-trust 

* Self-trust and humility can co-exist powerfully as “confident humility”: trust your ability to act, learn, and recover, while staying open to feedback, limits, and others’ wisdom. They reinforce each other—self-trust prevents humility from becoming self-doubt; humility prevents self-trust from becoming arrogance.

Thang 2 – Aggie Tennis Circuit (Cardio Burn)
Coupon-free speed round on the tennis court. AMRAP for ~10 minutes.
* 10 Merkins
* 10 Reverse Lunges each leg
* 10 Mountain Climbers (2-count) 
* 10 SSH
Shuffle the full perimeter of the tennis court after each round. 

More Q Source: Parallel Missions of Aggie Champions & F3
The Texas A&M women’s tennis team trusted each other, rotated leadership on the court, faced tough comebacks, and brought home the national title together.
That’s exactly what we do at F3. We embrace the suck, rotate the Q, leave no man behind, and get 1% better.

Keeping commitments is about one thing:
Trust.
When you keep commitments to others, you build trust with them

@D20 laid out a great plan and here are some points he put together…
 
Step 1: Find a goal in your job, your personal fitness, your home life that is realistic and attainable.

Step 2: Clear the path to your goal. Preparation is everything to help ensure success.

Step 3: Execute.

Step 4: Repeat from step 1 and find a new goal.

Step 5: You HC'ed and missed. You were going to run and woke up with a runny nose. You missed a deadline at work. Take ownership of the things you can. 

Step 6: Be kind to yourself and others. You screwed up. You're not a screw-up. Stay positive and get back up, dust yourself off, and do it again. You've got this.

Lean on your brothers, form a shield lock and realize you are not alone in this venture.

Q source: Self Trust
Men, true self-trust isn't some fake, hyped-up confidence we put on when we walk onto the court. Self-trust is simply the track record you have with yourself. It’s the belief that when you make a promise to the man in the mirror, you’re actually going to keep it.
​Think about why we are out here at 0530 on a Monday morning. When your alarm went off in the pitch black, you had a choice. If you get up, you build trust with yourself. If you hit snooze and roll over, you break it. Every time you push through a brutal round of Murph reps when your lungs are burning, you are depositing cash into your self-trust bank account.
​We talk a lot about being men that others can trust—our wives, our kids, our teams, the men that are here today. But you can't be a pillar for anyone else if your own foundation is shaky. If you can't trust yourself to follow through on the small commitments in the gloom, you won't trust yourself when life hits you with the heavy stuff in the daylight.
​Look at your track record today. If it’s good, keep building it. If it’s broken, start rebuilding it right now with the next repetition. Stop second-guessing your capabilities and start trusting the work you put in.

We talked about…
Keeping commitments is about one thing:
Trust.
When you keep commitments to others, you build trust with them
When you keep commitments to yourself, you build trust in yourself
And if a man doesn’t trust himself… everything else starts to wobble.

Question Becomes… where do we start if we currently aren’t there??

@D20 laid out a great plan and here are some points he put together…
 
Step 1: Find a goal in your job, your personal fitness, your home life that is realistic and attainable.

Step 2: Clear the path to your goal. Preparation is everything to help ensure success.

Step 3: Execute.

Step 4: Repeat from step 1 and find a new goal.

Step 5: You HC'ed and missed. You were going to run and woke up with a runny nose. You missed a deadline at work. Take ownership of the things you can. 

Step 6: Be kind to yourself and others. You screwed up. You're not a screw-up. Stay positive and get back up, dust yourself off, and do it again. You've got this.

Lean on your brothers, form a shield lock and realize you are not alone in this venture.

Question: How does uncertainty make you feel? How can you cultivate a healthy relationship with life's chaos?
To answer the 1st question, I've lived with uncertainty most of my life. All it caused was depression and anexity when I was younger because I believed that I had no future. We talked about…
Keeping commitments is about one thing:
Trust.
When you keep commitments to others, you build trust with them
When you keep commitments to yourself, you build trust in yourself
And if a man doesn’t trust himself… everything else starts to wobble.

Question Becomes… where do we start if we currently aren’t there??

@D20 laid out a great plan and here are some points he put together…
 
Step 1: Find a goal in your job, your personal fitness, your home life that is realistic and attainable.

Step 2: Clear the path to your goal. Preparation is everything to help ensure success.

Step 3: Execute.

Step 4: Repeat from step 1 and find a new goal.

Step 5: You HC'ed and missed. You were going to run and woke up with a runny nose. You missed a deadline at work. Take ownership of the things you can. 

Step 6: Be kind to yourself and others. You screwed up. You're not a screw-up. Stay positive and get back up, dust yourself off, and do it again. You've got this.

Lean on your brothers, form a shield lock and realize you are not alone in this venture.

Q source
Most men want certainty. A clear plan. Predictable outcomes. Control. But life rarely works that way. Leadership, fatherhood, marriage, work, health—almost all of the meaningful parts of life involve uncertainty. And for many men, that uncertainty creates anxiety, hesitation, frustration, or the feeling that they’re falling behind.
The problem is that if your peace depends on certainty, you’ll constantly feel unstable. There will always be variables you can’t control, outcomes you can’t guarantee, and situations you can’t fully predict.
That’s where self-trust comes in.

Self-trust is the belief that even if things become difficult, unclear, or chaotic, you can handle it. Not perfectly—but steadily. It’s confidence in your ability to adapt, respond, and continue moving forward without needing every answer ahead of time.
A healthy relationship with chaos doesn’t mean enjoying uncertainty or pretending hard things don’t affect you. It means learning not to panic when life gets unprerdictable. It means focusing on what you can control:
your effort
your attitude
your preparation
your response

Q Source: The easiest way to build more trust in yourself is by taking more responsibility in your life, your fitness, your job, your relationships, anything that gives you the chance to prove you can do what you say.  

Trust between two people is earned.  It is earned by keeping your commitments among other ways. It is earned by being dependable, by being reliable.  

Think back to the times when you couldn’t do something alone…. Move from one home to another. Get home because you were too drunk to drive. Survive the sleepness nights from a newborn. Fallen into some bad, if not self-destructive, habits.  Think about who was there for you.  Christ is always there for us, but we can be too stubborn or too resistance or feel unworthy.  In those moments, He will often put others in His place… to lift and help…. to provide a meal, to take a baby on a car ride so you can sleep, to get you home from too much liquor, to get your stuff on trucks to your new home.  It’s in these moments where trust forms. Think of the appreciation you have felt to others in those moments.  And think of the joy you have felt from being able to be the helping hand.  We are hard wired to serve others to one degree or another.  

But those feelings related to service don’t seem to extend to ourselves.  It can feel selfish.  It can even feel silly and insignificant.  But I would argue that it’s just as important, if not moreso, than committing to others.  It’s a sign of your own discipline, your own motivation, but more deeply, how you perceive your own self-worth.  When you lack self-trust, you may make commitments to others to seek validation or avoid conflict. This is considered a form of self-betrayal. When you trust yourself, you can consciously choose to commit to another, knowing that if things go wrong, you will not lose or abandon yourself. Trust in yourself grows when you keep tiny, daily promises (e.g., waking up on time, setting a boundary, doing a BD). We talked about…
Keeping commitments is about one thing:
Trust.
When you keep commitments to others, you build trust with them
When you keep commitments to yourself, you build trust in yourself
And if a man doesn’t trust himself… everything else starts to wobble.

Question Becomes… where do we start if we currently aren’t there??

@D20 laid out a great plan and here are some points he put together…
 
Step 1: Find a goal in your job, your personal fitness, your home life that is realistic and attainable.

Step 2: Clear the path to your goal. Preparation is everything to help ensure success.

Step 3: Execute.

Step 4: Repeat from step 1 and find a new goal.

Step 5: You HC'ed and missed. You were going to run and woke up with a runny nose. You missed a deadline at work. Take ownership of the things you can. 

Step 6: Be kind to yourself and others. You screwed up. You're not a screw-up. Stay positive and get back up, dust yourself off, and do it again. You've got this.

Lean on your brothers, form a shield lock and realize you are not alone in this venture.

Q-Source / Notes:
We talked about…
Keeping commitments is about one thing:
Trust.
When you keep commitments to others, you build trust with them
When you keep commitments to yourself, you build trust in yourself
And if a man doesn’t trust himself… everything else starts to wobble.

Question Becomes… where do we start if we currently aren’t there??

@D20 laid out a great plan and here are some points he put together…
 
Step 1: Find a goal in your job, your personal fitness, your home life that is realistic and attainable.

Step 2: Clear the path to your goal. Preparation is everything to help ensure success.

Step 3: Execute.

Step 4: Repeat from step 1 and find a new goal.

Step 5: You HC'ed and missed. You were going to run and woke up with a runny nose. You missed a deadline at work. Take ownership of the things you can. 

Step 6: Be kind to yourself and others. You screwed up. You're not a screw-up. Stay positive and get back up, dust yourself off, and do it again. You've got this.

Lean on your brothers, form a shield lock and realize you are not alone in this venture.

We talked about…
Keeping commitments is about one thing:
Trust.
When you keep commitments to others, you build trust with them
When you keep commitments to yourself, you build trust in yourself
And if a man doesn’t trust himself… everything else starts to wobble.

Question Becomes… where do we start if we currently aren’t there??

<band:refer user_key="AAC8jcSc6EYR_DIAVebZwrYM">D20</band:refer> laid out a great plan and here are some points he put together…
 
Step 1: Find a goal in your job, your personal fitness, your home life that is realistic and attainable.

Step 2: Clear the path to your goal. Preparation is everything to help ensure success.

Step 3: Execute.

Step 4: Repeat from step 1 and find a new goal.

Step 5: You HC'ed and missed. You were going to run and woke up with a runny nose. You missed a deadline at work. Take ownership of the things you can. 

Step 6: Be kind to yourself and others. You screwed up. You're not a screw-up. Stay positive and get back up, dust yourself off, and do it again. You've got this.

Lean on your brothers, form a shield lock and realize you are not alone in this venture.

Q source: Failing
Failing can be the worst thing in life or it can be the best. Some people don’t see failing as an option which is a great mentality to have, but what happens when you reach that destination? Do you give up and throw in the towel? The answer to my last question is no, you don't give up. Whatever may be challenging us may require more from us that we don’t have at the moment, whether that be patience, peace, wisdom, or discipline. 

Fail forward, not backwards. 

Failing backwards is giving up when things get hard, when life tells us we can't or it's not possible.

Failing forward is getting ready for the next attempt and preparing for the next failure until you finally accomplish what you set out to do.

It's being resilient and breaking walls down, one failure at a time. This isn't to encourage you to accept failure, but to let you know the fight isn't over until you decide to give up.

As a man of God, I don't claim victory of Perseverance alone. Jesus Christ is my Lord and Savior, deserving all the glory and my praise for everything good that has happened for me, and for what was meant for evil but turned into good that has happened to me.


There's no judgment if you are struggling with these same battles I've had, but I speak this truth from the experience I've had in my life.

I was chained to alcohol for 14 years, addicted to cigarettes in my early 20s, dealing with depression and anxiety, my life slowly failing backwards because I thought it was over, until I surrendered my life to Jesus, I saw His light in my dark world. In the midst of failing, I was covered by His Grace. Giving me chance after chance until I finally got it right. I am redeemed with purpose to lead others in knowing how great God is.  
Stay relentlessly and trust in HIM.

Question of the Week: Do we always have to face our fears?  

The short answer is no; we don’t.  As Linked In has talked about, it is not necessary to face fears that are rational, keep you safe, or do not hinder your well-being.  Fear of getting burned from putting our hand on a hot stove is not something we need to do as it proves nothing.  Avoiding fears often intensifies them.  Facing fears—often through slow gradual exposure—will help us to become 1% better. Stepping into fear can truly be a transformative process that can build confidence, broaden your life, and bring joy that you might not otherwise feel. It brings strength and faith in yourself, God, and, through the example that you show, brings strength and faith to those around you.  

I will argue that there absolutely are fears – on whatever level and to whatever extent -  that can lead to complacency, mediocrity, and the inability to act.  It limits what we do, how others see us, and, more importantly, how we see ourselves. Fear can lead to lack of confidence and self-worth. Fear is a disease.  It affects our minds, altering the way we think and perceive the world around us, and physically hurts our cardiovascular health and immune systems… potentially creating a constant state of sickness. This disease can hamper us from the important activities of daily living.   Having said that, it is necessary, even vital, to confront fears to overcome anxieties and stop them from limiting your life.  

I challenge each of you to find one fear in your life.  Just one. And take steps through small gradual steps to eliminate that fear.  

Think about this… If we could literally reach into you and remove all your fears – every one of them – how different would your life be? Think about it. If nothing stopped you from following your dreams, your life would probably be very different.

Self-trust is basically your internal reputation. It's the quiet belief that 'if I say I'll do
something, i t gets done." Without that, everything else discipline, confidence, leadership starts to wobble.
Keeping commitments, both to yourself and to others, matters for a few big reasons:
1. It builds identity, not just results
Every time you follow through—whether it's a workout, a promise, or a deadline-you
reinforce a simple identity: I'm someone who does what I say. That compounds. Miss enough of those, and the opposite identity forms just as fast.
2. It reduces internal friction
When you don't trust yourself, everything becomes a negotiation. You second-guess plans,
delay decisions, and burn energy convincing yourself to act. Self-trust removes that noise
—you decide, then execute.
3 . It strengthens discipline under pressure
Motivation is unreliable. Commitment is what carries you when you're tired, busy, o r not
feeling it. Keeping small promises trains you to show up even when conditions aren't ideal.
4. It builds credibility with others
People track consistency more than intentions. If you follow through, others rely on you
more, give you more responsibility, and trust your word. I f not, even good intentions start
to carry less weight.
5. It aligns your values with your actions
Most people say they value things like health, family, o r growth. Keeping commitments is
how those values become real instead o f just aspirational.
That said, blind consistency isn't the goal. There's a difference between:
• Breaking a commitment because you're avoiding discomfort, and
Renegotiating a commitment because circumstances genuinely changed
Self-trust actually improves when you make realistic commitments and adjust them
honestly-not when you overpromise and repeatedly miss.

Human relationships need trust to function. When I keep my commitments to you, you can trust that I'm going to do what I say I'm going to do. When I keep my commitments, I also build trust in myself - that I can do the things that I say I'm going to do. Every commitment that I keep - especially the hard ones - is a way of having my own back. I don't just think I'm reliable, I know that I am. That doesn't require external validation or approval, it just requires showing up when I say I will. You build yourself up with every commitment you keep.

And the commitments you don't keep? We're all human. We all fail. Some days you're building up, some days you're starting over. Don't give yourself permission to fail, but give yourself grace when you do. Then turn around and share that attitude with others. They're going to fail, just like you did. It's not ok to fail, but it is ok to forgive ourselves and others when we fail. The failure isn't the important part. What you do next is what's important. Is failure the fuel that helps you keep your next commitment, or a belief that you're the kind of person that doesn't show up? Just know that only the former builds trust in yourself, and if you don't trust yourself, no one else will either. Self-trust is the kind of internal quality that projects. It doesn't show up as loud and brash, but quiet and unshakeable.

### THANG 1 — Workout Relay (4 Groups, 3 Stations)

PAX broke into **4 groups**. Each group had **3 rotating stations:**

|Station             |Exercise                                                           
**Front (Leader)**|Parachute sprint — 100 yards to cones, touch, sprint back          |
**Middle**        |Speed ladder — 2 feet in each rung, continuous until leader returns|
**Back**          |Jump rope                                                          

**Rotation:** When the parachute runner returns → tags the front of the ladder line → runner grabs jump rope → jump roper joins the ladder group.

**Al Gore** (air squat hold) for the six until all PAX complete their round.

*2 rounds completed**

### THANG 2 — Indian Run

- PAX formed **2 lines** and jogged around the park complex
- Last person in line **sprints to the front** and becomes the new leader
- Continues until every PAX has had a sprint turn

✅ **Full lap completed — break taken**

### THANG 3 — Hill Relay at Wolf Pen (Same 4 Groups)

Groups reformed. **3 stations, hill format:**

|Station             |Exercise

**Rotation:** Finish your hill run → go straight into Bernie Sanders → Bernie joins the sit-up group.

✅ **2 rounds. It was EXHAUSTING.**

This morning, 9 HIMS mustarded with YHC in the gloom to push back against sad clown syndrome and to honor the ragtag Texian forces who sacrificed for the Republic of Texas. We weren’t about to let the weather—or the sweat and effort required—keep us from getting 1% better or from remembering the Alamo. Along the way, we also confronted fears that can limit us as leaders.

Looking back at Texas history, it’s hard to imagine the level of fear those Texian soldiers carried. News of the fall of the Alamo and the massacre at Goliad spread quickly, along with reports of other battles. Sam Houston continued to retreat, buying time to train his army so they’d be ready to execute when the moment came. In times like that, you have to dig deep and stand firm in your principles to overcome fear. If we let fear take hold, it can paralyze us—and that often leads to failure. I’ll admit, the fear of failure is a strong motivator for me, maybe more than I care to acknowledge. It’s not just failing myself, but the idea of letting others down that can weigh heavily.

One thing I’m working to instill in my boys is that when I say I’m going to do something or be somewhere, it matters. My word should mean something. At the same time, I want them to understand that actions have consequences, and losing a privilege should carry weight too. I don’t always get that balance right, but I’m trying. At the end of the day, we’re all human—and we’re all learning as we go.

Thang 1 Lindsays aka 40’s— Dips/Curls for the Girls
Lindsays are a high-rep variation of Elevens. You start with 30 reps of one exercise and 10 reps of another exercise OYO, then subtract 5 reps from the first exercise and add five reps from the second. Repeat OYO until you have 10 reps of the first exercise and 30 reps of the second. The sum must always add up to 40. Example: Lindsays with Dips and Curls for the girls starts you with 30 Dips and 10 Curls, then 25 Dips and 15 Curls, then 20 Dips and 20 Curls, then 15 Dips and 25 Curls, then 10 Dips and 30 Curls.

“Every man out here has something that sets him off.
A comment.
A tone.
A certain kind of person.
That’s called a trigger.”

“Weak men blame their triggers on other people.
‘He made me mad.’
‘She disrespected me.’
‘That guy always sets me off.’
Strong men don’t do that.”

“Strong men get curious about their triggers.”

“They ask:
Why did that hit me like that?
Why does that get under my skin?
What’s really going on in me?”
“Because the truth is…
your trigger isn’t about them.”

“It’s about you.”

“Ownership doesn’t mean you never get triggered.
That’s not real life.”
“It means you don’t let it run the show.”
“It might look like this:
‘Hey… give me five minutes. I’m not ready to answer that well yet.’”

“That’s not weakness.
That’s control.”

“Out here, when things get hard, you feel it.
Frustration. Fatigue. Irritation.”
“Some guys snap.
Some guys shut down.”
“But the ones who grow?
They lean in and take ownership.”

“Your triggers will show up.
That’s a guarantee.”
“The question is…

do they control you… or do you own them?”

Theme: Since my F3 Nickname is Neon Moon, today’s theme is about NASA’s Artemis II mission to the moon. 

Fact: Artemis II flew over 700,000 miles over 10 days, and 4,600 miles beyond the far side of the Moon – the farthest any humans have traveled since 1972 (54 years). 

Thang 1 – 3 orbits of 54 reps
Grab cindies in double applesauce formation and complete reps of the following, staying in formation between each station:

•  13 Block Overhead Presses (basketball court)

Fact: On April 10, 2026, Artemis II’s capsule Orion re-entered Earth’s atmosphere at over 24,500 mph (with temperatures reaching ~2,200°C) and splashed down safely in the Pacific Ocean off San Diego, fully validating the heat shield and recovery procedures with a crew aboard.

Q Source: the Parallel Missions of Artemis II & F3
Artemis II successfully sent four astronauts on a journey around the Moon and safely back to Earth. With no quick rescue possible, the astronauts had to trust each other completely. They rotated leadership roles fluidly, faced extreme discomfort, communication blackouts, a blazing re-entry — and they brought the mission home together.
That is exactly what we do here at F3.
We show up in the gloom and choose to embrace the suck because that’s where growth lives. We leave no man behind, but we also refuse to leave any man where we found him. Every one of us rotates through the Q spot — stepping up to lead, just like the Artemis II crew rotated command responsibilities. We expand the circle and invite all men in, regardless of where they’re starting from. And we do it shoulder-to-shoulder, because shared suffering and shared laughter forge bonds that turn hard things into something meaningful.
The mission isn’t just to get stronger — it’s to get 1% better together, build better men, and strengthen the communities we return to every day.
So today we show up here in the gloom with purpose. We push ourselves and the men beside us. We laugh through the burn. Because that’s what high-impact men do.

•  Minute 2: MAX Speed High Knees (sprinting through the atmosphere)

I was asked to discuss self reflection but more importantly about repentance and how the two work hand in hand. 

Self-reflection and repentance are related but different: self-reflection helps you identify your thoughts and shortcomings, while repentance is the action of turning away from them and toward God by confessing your sins. 

Key idea: reflection diagnoses the problem; repentance is the solution.

Self-reflection looks inward and can lead to awareness or even regret, but it doesn’t create change on its own. Repentance involves a deeper shift—acknowledging wrong, feeling genuine conviction, and making a decisive change in direction.

Together, they form a cycle of growth: you reflect, recognize what needs to change, and then actively turn and grow through repentance.

Something I personally need to reflect and repent on to help you think about this in your own life: Presence with my family. Asking god for the ability to disconnect from work and stay off my phone and away from distractions. Question of the Week: Can fear be healthy?  If so, when does it stop being healthy.  If not, why not?  

Courtesy of Linked In.  If you haven’t read this yet, you are missing out.  Do yourself a big favor and read it.  It’s long, but I know you can do it.  Even Narc can read it.  

First: Can fear be healthy?
Yes. Fear is not the villain… it’s the smoke alarm.
At its best, fear is a signal, not a sentence.
It keeps you from stepping into traffic
It sharpens your awareness under pressure
It forces preparation before a hard thing
There’s a reason even elite operators, athletes, and leaders still feel fear. They just use it as fuel instead of letting it grab the steering wheel.


“Fear is a tool. If it’s in your hand, it helps you. If it’s in your head, it controls you.”


When does fear stop being healthy?
Fear turns from guardian → jailer when:
1. It starts making decisions for you
You avoid the hard conversation
You don’t take the shot
You shrink instead of rise
2. It becomes chronic instead of situational
Healthy fear spikes and fades.
Unhealthy fear lingers like background static.
3. It disconnects you from your purpose
In F3 terms:
It pulls you away from Fitness (you stop pushing)
It weakens Fellowship (you isolate)
It dulls Faith (you stop trusting something bigger)


“Fear is unhealthy when it costs you the man you’re supposed to be.”


Do we always have to face our fears?

No… but also yes.

Not every fear deserves a showdown:
You don’t need to “face” a fear of touching a hot stove
Some fears are just wisdom in work boots
But the fears tied to:
Growth
Responsibility
Leadership
Calling

…those fears you must face, or they quietly shape your life anyway.

“The fears that guard your potential are the ones you have to walk toward.”

“Every man here is afraid of something.
Not being enough. Failing. Being exposed. Losing control.
But fear doesn’t disqualify you.
Letting it decide your life does.
The goal isn’t to eliminate fear.
The goal is to outgrow its authority.”
If the answer points toward shrinking… it’s time to move.

THANG 1 – Sloth Climb Rail Plank 
Waiting Pax do following core circuit on repeat
10 BBSU

10 Wedding Nights

Pax 1 starts up the stairs
Sloth railing climb
Sit on bottom step. Grab rail from underneath, lift your 6 off the ground, and pull yourself up the rail, hand over hand, like a sloth climbing along hanging from a branch. Use your feet to help you climb the stairs, you’re working your upper body and core. 
At landing, stand up and run to about 4 steps from top of the landing and then lean forward, hold onto both rails in an iron cross incline plank position, and then yell GO to the next Pax for them to go. 
Pax 2 starts up the stairs with sloth climb, runs to Pax 1 and takes Pax 1’s spot doing the incline railing plank, and yells for Pax 3 to start. 
Pax 1 repeats the sloth climb 1 flight, run 1 flight and railing plank. 
Alternate inside rail and outside rail on Sloth climbs so you work both sides of your body. 
Pax 3 starts when called with sloth climb, run, tags Pax 2 and takes Pax 2’s spot in railing plank, and Pax 2 sloth climbs, runs to tag Pax 1.
Pax 1 continues to holler when they reach their next hold point. 
As Pax reach the top, continue core exercises. 
Holler out at top landing. As each Pax reaches top, holler and last Pax in line will move up to keep the cycle flowing. 
When Pax arrive at top, continue core exercises until 6 is in.

First: Can fear be healthy?
Yes. Fear is not the villain… it’s the smoke alarm.
At its best, fear is a signal, not a sentence.
It keeps you from stepping into traffic
It sharpens your awareness under pressure
It forces preparation before a hard thing
There’s a reason even elite operators, athletes, and leaders still feel fear. They just use it as fuel instead of letting it grab the steering wheel.


“Fear is a tool. If it’s in your hand, it helps you. If it’s in your head, it controls you.”


When does fear stop being healthy?
Fear turns from guardian → jailer when:
1. It starts making decisions for you
You avoid the hard conversation
You don’t take the shot
You shrink instead of rise
2. It becomes chronic instead of situational
Healthy fear spikes and fades.
Unhealthy fear lingers like background static.
3. It disconnects you from your purpose
In F3 terms:
It pulls you away from Fitness (you stop pushing)
It weakens Fellowship (you isolate)
It dulls Faith (you stop trusting something bigger)


“Fear is unhealthy when it costs you the man you’re supposed to be.”


Do we always have to face our fears?

No… but also yes.

Not every fear deserves a showdown:
You don’t need to “face” a fear of touching a hot stove
Some fears are just wisdom in work boots
But the fears tied to:
Growth
Responsibility
Leadership
Calling

…those fears you must face, or they quietly shape your life anyway.

“The fears that guard your potential are the ones you have to walk toward.”

“Every man here is afraid of something.
Not being enough. Failing. Being exposed. Losing control.
But fear doesn’t disqualify you.
Letting it decide your life does.
The goal isn’t to eliminate fear.
The goal is to outgrow its authority.”
If the answer points toward shrinking… it’s time to move.

Q Source: 
Healthy fear keeps you alive. I’m not afraid of those big orb weaver spiders. They might look intimidating, but they’re harmless. I don’t particularly LIKE running through spiderwebs that I can’t see before sunrise, but I don’t worry about them either. I got bitten by a brown recluse once. I do not put my bare hands or feet into wood piles in places that I can’t see are clear of widows and recluses. I have an entirely reasonable fear of accidentally invading that animal’s living space and unintentionally provoking a reaction.

Unhealthy fear keeps you stuck. Almost every conflict that you avoid instead of face will eventually have to be repaid with interest that compounds over time. Don’t let fear of someone else’s reaction keep you from doing what you need to do. As men, we’re called to lead. Good leaders work through conflict rather than trying to avoid it.

Don’t let fear define you. “I’m an anxious person.” “I’m not someone who speaks up.” “I don’t handle conflict well.” When fear becomes a story you tell about yourself, it stops becoming information and becomes a cage.

When fear protects your values, listen. When fear protects your life (but not at the cost of your values), pay attention. When fear protects your comfort, the status quo, or your sense of normalcy, it’s time to break free and grow.

Q source 
If you hold to your standards, you won't always be liked. For some men, the fear of not being liked is a major Obstacle. How can we overcome that, or help others overcome it?

The Obstacle
Most men don’t actually struggle with having standards—they struggle with needing approval. It shows up in small ways: avoiding hard conversations, softening the truth, letting things slide that shouldn’t, all in the name of keeping the peace. Being liked feels safe. There’s no conflict, no tension, no risk of rejection. But that safety comes at a cost. If you prioritize being liked, you eventually lose respect—especially your own. And once that starts to slip, everything else follows.

The real tension isn’t between being liked and being a good man. It’s between being liked in the moment and being respected over time. Those are two very different paths. Most people will choose the short-term comfort without realizing they’re trading away long-term credibility and leadership.

Q-source
The Way Through
It starts with getting clear on what you actually stand for. If you don’t define your standards, you’ll default to whatever the room expects of you. From there, you have to learn to detach from immediate reactions. The awkward silence, the pushback, someone being upset—that’s where most men fold. But you’re not responsible for how others react; you’re responsible for holding your line.

That doesn’t mean being harsh or aggressive. It means being direct, calm, and consistent. Over time, people may not always like it, but they will trust it. And trust is what builds real influence. This is a long game. In the moment, it may cost you approval. But in the long run, it earns you respect—and that’s what leadership actually requires.

And when you see another man wavering, don’t ignore it. Call him up, not out. A simple question can reset him: “Are you trying to be liked right now, or are you standing on what you said?” Because if you’re always liked, you’re probably not leading.

If you hold to your standards, you won't always be liked. For some men, the fear of not being liked is a major Obstacle. How can we overcome that, or help others overcome it?
The Obstacle
Most men don’t actually struggle with having standards—they struggle with needing approval. It shows up in small ways: avoiding hard conversations, softening the truth, letting things slide that shouldn’t, all in the name of keeping the peace. Being liked feels safe. There’s no conflict, no tension, no risk of rejection. But that safety comes at a cost. If you prioritize being liked, you eventually lose respect—especially your own. And once that starts to slip, everything else follows.
The real tension isn’t between being liked and being a good man. It’s between being liked in the moment and being respected over time. Those are two very different paths. Most people will choose the short-term comfort without realizing they’re trading away long-term credibility and leadership.

The Way Through
It starts with getting clear on what you actually stand for. If you don’t define your standards, you’ll default to whatever the room expects of you. From there, you have to learn to detach from immediate reactions. The awkward silence, the pushback, someone being upset—that’s where most men fold. But you’re not responsible for how others react; you’re responsible for holding your line.
That doesn’t mean being harsh or aggressive. It means being direct, calm, and consistent. Over time, people may not always like it, but they will trust it. And trust is what builds real influence. This is a long game. In the moment, it may cost you approval. But in the long run, it earns you respect—and that’s what leadership actually requires.
And when you see another man wavering, don’t ignore it. Call him up, not out. A simple question can reset him: “Are you trying to be liked right now, or are you standing on what you said?” Because if you’re always liked, you’re probably not leading.

Qsource
If you hold to your standards, you won't always be liked. For some men, the fear of not being liked is a major Obstacle. How can we overcome that, or help others overcome it?



That fear is more common than most men admit. Being liked feels safe—it signals belonging. But if you make it your main compass, you end up negotiating against your own values. The goal isn’t to stop caring what people think (that’s unrealistic), but to stop letting it decide your behavior.
Here’s how to work through it in a grounded, practical way:

1. Get clear on your standards (or you’ll default to approval)
A lot of people say they “have standards,” but in the moment they fold because those standards aren’t concrete.
Define them ahead of time:
	•	What do you tolerate in friendships, work, dating?
	•	What will you say no to—even if it costs you approval?
If you don’t pre-decide, your brain will choose the path of least social resistance.

2. Reframe rejection: it’s not always a loss
Not being liked often means one of three things:
	•	You set a boundary
	•	You expressed a real opinion
	•	You didn’t play a role someone expected
Those aren’t failures—they’re filters. You’re narrowing toward people who actually fit you.

3. Build tolerance for discomfort (this is the real skill)
The fear isn’t logical—it’s emotional. You have to train your nervous system, not just your mindset.
Start small:
	•	Say “no” to something low-stakes
	•	Disagree politely in a conversation
	•	Don’t over-explain a decision
You’re teaching yourself: nothing catastrophic happens when I’m not liked.

4. Watch for “approval-seeking behaviors”
These often fly under the radar:
	•	Over-explaining yourself
	•	Agreeing when you don’t mean it
	•	Avoiding necessary conflict
	•	Constantly softening your opinions
Catch them in real time and adjust. Even small corrections build self-respect.

5. Separate being respected from being liked
Being liked is often about comfort. Being respected is about consistency and boundaries.
Ironically, people tend to respect (and often eventually like) those who:
	•	Are clear about what they stand for
	•	Don’t bend under pressure
	•	Treat themselves as someone worth respecting

6. Help others by modeling, not preaching
If you want to help other men with this:
	•	Show them what it looks like to say “no” calmly
	•	Back your words with consistent actions
	•	Don’t shame them for struggling with it
People change faster by example than by advice.

7. Accept the trade-off (this is the hard truth)
You can be:
	•	Widely liked but vaguely respected or
	•	Selectively liked but deeply respected
Trying to maximize both usually leads to being neither.

If you hold to your standards, you won't always be liked. For some men, the fear of not being liked is a major Obstacle. How can we overcome that, or help others overcome it? 
One of the first things that came to my mind in this regard is having good community around you. Another point brought up in brief discussion: if you are part of a group, the group has standards for each of the members to hold up. The Standard: Here’s the uncomfortable truth about upholding a standard: most people swing between two bad modes
	1.	“I have standards” → becomes rigid, judgmental, exhausting
	2.	“I respect others” → becomes a doormat with vibes instead of boundaries

The trick is holding both at once without making it everyone else’s problem.

1. Define standards as personal filters, not universal laws

Your standards are about what you accept in your life, not what’s objectively “right.”
* “I don’t stay in relationships where communication is inconsistent”
* NOT “People who don’t text back quickly are inconsiderate”
* One is a boundary. The other is a personality flaw disguised as a philosophy.

2. Separate observation from interpretation.  
People behave a certain way. Then we add a dramatic story on top.
* Observation: “They canceled twice last minute.
* Interpretation: “They don’t respect me.”
* Maybe true. Maybe they’re just chaotic. Your move shouldn’t depend on being right about their soul.

3. Act on patterns, not single moments. 
If your “standards” react to every annoyance, you don’t have standards. You have mood swings.
* One bad day → let it go
* Repeated behavior → adjust access
* Consistency is what makes a boundary real.

4. Quiet enforcement beats loud declarations. 
You don’t need a TED Talk every time someone crosses a line.

Instead of:
* “I have a boundary around my time and emotional labor…”
* Try: Stop over-accommodating, Say no once, clearly; Then follow through. 
* People learn from what changes, not what you announce.

5. Respect doesn’t mean unlimited access. 
This is where people get confused.

You can:
* Respect someone’s choices
* AND decide those choices don’t work for you. 
* That’s not judgment. That’s selection.

6. Drop the fantasy of fixing people. 
* Rebuilding standards usually comes after realizing you tolerated too much, then trying to “manage” others into better behavior.
* That never works long-term.
* Standards = choosing, not coaching.

7. Expect some friction. 
If you raise your standards, a few people will: Push back; Guilt-trip; Drift away. That’s not failure. That’s the system updating.

People sometimes let others trample over their standards for several reasons. One major reason is the fear of conflict. Many people would rather avoid arguments or tension, so they stay quiet even when someone crosses a boundary. Another reason is the desire to be liked or accepted. When we care about maintaining relationships or fitting in, we might lower our standards to keep the peace. Low self-worth can also play a role, because someone who doubts their value may feel they do not deserve to have their standards respected.
Allowing others to repeatedly break our standards can have negative effects on us over time. It can slowly damage our self-respect because we feel like we are not standing up for ourselves. It can also lead to resentment toward the people who keep crossing those boundaries. In the long run, it may create unhealthy relationships where one person takes advantage of the other. This is why having clear boundaries and communicating them is important, since healthy relationships should involve mutual respect.

Entered this weeks Q Source question into ChatGPT. Not bad. One thing that's interesting is it went straight to boundaries. I didn't put that in the question. While we go through this, don't forget what @ltDangle said last week - boundaries aren't necessarily walls. We need to see them as bridges to build between each other. All of the examples below have merit, I personally like 6 and 7 the best. 
🧭 Why we let people trample our standards
Even strong, capable people slip into this sometimes. Here are the most common reasons:

1. Fear of conflict
Many people worry that saying “no” will:
* Create tension
* Make someone upset
* Lead to retaliation or distance
Avoiding conflict feels easier in the moment, but it comes at a cost.

2. Wanting acceptance or approval
We’re social creatures. A lot of us unconsciously trade our standards for:
* Belonging
* Harmony
* Being seen as “easygoing,” “helpful,” or “nice”
Over time, this approval can become more valuable to us than our own boundaries.

3. Low self-worth or self-doubt
When someone isn’t sure they’re deserving of respect, they will:
* Set weak boundaries
* Let things slide
* Rationalize someone else’s mistreatment
It’s not weakness — it’s conditioning.

4. Habit
If you’re used to being the caretaker, the problem-solver, or the dependable one, your mind automatically:
* Prioritizes others
* Downplays your needs
* Tolerates behavior you shouldn’t
Old roles are hard to break.

5. Emotional attachment
With family, close friends, partners, or long‑term coworkers, we often:
* Give more chances than we should
* Excuse behavior
* Hope things will “get better”
Attachment can dilute accountability.

6. Confusion about what your standards actually are
Sometimes people can’t defend their standards because they haven’t clearly defined them. Vague boundaries lead to:
* inconsistent reactions
* letting things go “just this once”
* being talked out of your own feelings

7. Exhaustion
When you’re overwhelmed, it becomes easy to say:
* “Fine, whatever.”
* “I don’t have the energy to fight this.”
Burnout makes boundary-breaking feel inevitable.

💥 What it does to us
Letting people step over our standards isn’t neutral — it leaves a mark.

1. Resentment builds up
Even if you stay quiet, your mind keeps score. Over time you feel:
* Irritated
* Drained
* Unappreciated
Resentment is the emotional debt of unspoken boundaries.

2. You lose trust in yourself
When you violate your own standards, the brain interprets it as:
* “My needs don’t matter.”
* “Other people decide what I tolerate.”
Self-trust erodes each time you abandon a boundary.

3. Your identity blurs
Standards shape who you are. When you soften them for others:
* You feel disconnected from yourself
* You don’t recognize your own behavior
* You feel like you’re living someone else’s life

4. People stop respecting you
Not necessarily out of malice — but people follow the rules you enforce. If you:
* tolerate disrespect
* reward inconsistency
* keep saying “it’s fine”
…people adapt their behavior to that.

5. Emotional exhaustion and burnout
Carrying everyone else’s emotional load while burying your own creates:
* Anxiety
* Stress
* Fatigue
* Low motivation
Your system is running beyond design.

6. Long-term dissatisfaction
When your standards crumble, so does your sense of direction. People describe feeling:
* Checked out
* Numb
* Stuck
* Frustrated
It becomes harder to feel proud of your decisions or your relationships.

🌱 The encouraging part
This pattern is reversible. And once you understand why it’s happening, you can start rebuilding boundaries that reflect the person you actually want to be.

You all just did something hard. You held a standard for yourself and for the guy next to you.

Now think about the last time you let somebody else lower yours.

Maybe it was at work. A meeting where something got decided that you knew was wrong, and you didn't say anything. Maybe it was at home: you let something slide because you were tired, or you didn't want the fight. Maybe it was with yourself. You made a commitment and let someone talk you out of it or you let their comfort become more important than your conviction.

Why do we do that? Usually it's one of three things: we want to be liked, we want to avoid conflict, or we've decided somewhere along the line that our standards were actually optional.

Here's what that costs. Every time you let someone walk across your line without consequence, the line moves. And after a while, you forget where it was. You don't lose your standards all at once. You negotiate them away, one small surrender at a time.

Q-source:  
"A man with no enemies stands for nothing." What are the standards you base your life on? 
To the best of my ability, I try to make my standards based on what is in the Bible and on the teachings of Jesus since I am a follower of Jesus. 
I think that standards are like anchors - they keep us steady as the world around us changes. Sometimes, I think of our lives and our personal development in the context of a flat character arc. This also stems from one of the things that the Bible says about God which is that He is the same yesterday, today, and forever. In a way, that is reminiscent of a flat character arc - a protagonist that is so steady, so well-rooted in what is true and right and in their convictions, that even as the world changes and culture sways between two extremes, the protagonist stays steady. And that creates tension, and the tension can also create enemies from different places as the times change. A great point was also brought up in discussion that we, as fallible creatures, need to hold our convictions with humility. We could be wrong and could have bad standards, so we need to be able to admit when we need to correct them. Standards also do not necessarily fix our behavior for all time, but as times change it may affect how we interact with the world around us even though our convictions and the principles by which we live may remain consistent. 
Along with answering "what are your standards," I think it's also important to answer the question of "what voices speak loudest and/or most consistently in your life"? Even without realizing it, the voices that we give the most air time to will unconsciously shape and shift our standards. As such, we need to be careful about what we let into our hearts and minds.

F3 Aggieland — The Cave
Guest Q: RoadRash (F3 Alliance) Total PAX: 19 (including 2 FNGs) + 2 DD

Iron Goose Invasion — Double Down Pre-Runs

The gloom belonged to the committed.
At 0430, two PAX stepped off into an eerily quiet College Station for the first Iron Goose Double Down. Five miles. Empty roads. No applause. Just discipline.

At 0530, a second wave launched from The Cave — one man logging three miles, another pushing six.
While the pavement pounders were stacking miles, Whistleblower led the brave in a Sandbag Double Down. 

Before most alarms sounded, work had already been done.

0630 — Beatdown Commences
We circled up. The F3 Mission was recited:
To plant, grow, and serve small workout groups for men for the invigoration of male community leadership.
The Five Core Principles were spoken clearly:
	•	Free of charge
	•	Open to all men
	•	Held outdoors, rain or shine, heat or cold
	•	Led in a rotating fashion by men who participate
	•	Ends in a Circle of Trust
Disclaimer delivered.
We counted off.
Eighteen.
Pause.
A late arrival stepped into the circle — no man turned away in the gloom. We counted again.
Nineteen PAX ready to work.
Two FNGs were identified and assigned battle buddies.

Warm-Up
Motivators from five. Little baby arm circles. Flapjacks. Michael Phelps. Grass grabbers. Short. Direct. Intentional.

Then YHC explained what was coming.

The Thang — OYO BOMB Ladder (Narrative)
YHC laid out the cones at 100 yards and explained that this would be an OYO BOMB ladder — simple in structure, relentless in execution. From the start line, each man would sprint to the first cone and complete one burpee, two overhead claps, three merkins, four big boy sit-ups, and five squats. Then it was a hard sprint back to the start, turn immediately, and attack the second cone for two, four, six, eight, and ten. Each cone increased the count, climbing steadily all the way down the field. 

The structure was straightforward, but the accumulation was not. Lungs burned early. Legs tightened quickly. The Celtic punk playlist drove the cadence as bagpipes and grit filled the air. It was OYO, but it was never alone. 

The men who finished early circled back to pick up the six. No man left behind. No man left where you found him. Every PAX crossed the line inside the hour, ground down but stronger than when they started.

Name-O-Rama
Two FNGs earned their names:
Dozer. Predator.
Welcome to the brotherhood.

COT — “Pressure Makes Men” (Narrative)
YHC brought the men in tight and let the silence settle before speaking. I told them that what we just did was not simply a workout — it was pressure. Pressure does not destroy a man; it reveals him. No one needs F3 to get in shape. A man can run alone, lift alone, suffer alone. But alone is exactly how men fall apart. F3 exists because isolated men become weak men, and weak men create hard lives for everyone around them. I reminded them that each of us sits at the center of a blast radius. Our attitude hits our wives. Our discipline hits our kids. Our character hits our coworkers. Our presence hits our communities. When the man in the center gets better, everything gets better. Scripture tells us in 1 Corinthians 16:13 to be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, and be strong. Not act like boys. Not act like victims. Act like men. I challenged them with a simple truth: their families do not care how fast they ran this morning. They care who walks through the door tonight. Do they get the best version of you, or the leftovers after stress and comfort have taken their toll? Every man standing there knows someone who needs this — not wants it, needs it. Stressed. Drifting. Angry. Numb. Alone. And he will not show up unless someone goes to get him. Somebody did that for you. Nobody wakes up at 5 a.m. by accident. I closed by reminding them that today we dropped BOMBS not to tear men down, but to clear weakness so something stronger can be built. The world does not need more comfortable men. It needs dangerous men who choose to be good. If you do not lead your life, something else will.

Honored to bring the pressure to The Cave.
— RoadRash

Q Source
This weeks’ Q source pertains to presence and what that means in repairing relationships.  

“I would contend that the relationship you have with you, the fight against the baggage, the voices, the triggers, the demons seems like it would be the easiest to repair because there’s no interference, the communication can flow more easily than with “other” people because finding the right words isn’t as much a part of the communication process.  But that repair with yourself between you and yourself lends may be the one where communication, and being present, might actually be the hardest.  Giving yourself the time and space to talk with YOU while kids are fighting, or the debate about how to load the dishwasher continues, with screens and phones pulling at you, and don’t forget to do that thing you just remembered before your noon appointment can quickly take over.  And that fight, that demon, may be getting stronger all the time so the fight. needs to be had.  Brothers, I would content that fighting that fight is important and giving yourself that space to fight that fight against the demons often cannot be done alone.  Do something good for yourself every day, every morning to make yourself 1% each day so that fight you fight alone can be fought and won. I would also contend that that fight is best done with those you do hard things with, with those who see you, your character.  We in the gloom see you, connect with you by doing hard things together, and because we do hard things together, bringing those demons into COT, bringing them here, I testify will make you 1% better, at least. Presence is the difference between handing someone a scripted apology… and actually standing in the room with them.

Repairs only work when the other person feels seen. And that requires Presence.

Here’s how Presence affects your ability to repair:

1. Presence forces ownership
When you are fully present, you cannot hide behind busyness, sarcasm, or deflection. You feel the weight of what happened. Presence strips away spin. A distracted man explains. A present man owns.

2. Presence slows you down
Most failed repairs happen because we rush to fix the discomfort instead of the damage. Presence creates pause. It allows you to listen instead of defend. To absorb instead of react. That pause is where trust begins to rebuild.

3. Presence lets the other person feel felt
People don’t need perfect words. They need to feel understood. If your eyes are scanning the room or your mind is building your rebuttal, they know. Presence communicates, “You matter more than my pride.”

4. Presence regulates emotion
If you are not grounded, you cannot repair. When you’re present, you can hold tension without escaping it. You don’t escalate. You don’t collapse. You stay steady. That steadiness is strength.

5. Presence turns apology into connection

A repair isn’t a transaction. It’s a bridge. Presence transforms “Sorry about that” into “I see how I hurt you, and I care enough to sit here in it with you.”

A distracted man tries to win the argument.

A present man tries to win the relationship.

Presence is costly. It requires humility. It requires time. It requires being uncomfortable.

But without it, repairs are just words.

With it, repairs become welds.

If you want a question to land the plane in your COT:

“When I make a mistake, do I rush to clear my name… or do I slow down long enough to repair the connection?”

QSOURCE
* Fitness = mood regulation.
The workouts are not just about abs you’ll never see again after 40. Regular exertion lowers stress hormones and boosts mood. Showing up at 5:30a.m. is a vote against isolation.
* Showing up matters more than crushing it.
Some days you PR. Some days you just survive burpees. Consistency beats intensity for mental stability.
* Fellowship = accountability.
Men tend to isolate when struggling. F3 bakes in connection. If you miss a few workouts, someone notices. That is not surveillance. That is protection.
* Surface talk leads to real talk.
The parking lot chatter and post-workout coffee are where “I’m good” sometimes turns into “Actually, I’m not.” That’s the gold.
* Shared suffering builds trust.
Doing hard things together lowers the barrier to honest conversations. It’s weirdly easier to talk about anxiety when you just did bear crawls in the dark.
* Faith = purpose.
Whether that’s traditional faith or simply believing your life serves something bigger than your job title, purpose is a mental health stabilizer. Drift is dangerous.
* Leadership is service, not image.
Leading a workout or checking on a guy who’s been absent reinforces meaning. Helping someone else is one of the fastest ways to pull yourself out of your own head.

Q-Source - Presence
Discuss some distractions that hurt our presence (Social media, phones, work) and strategies for minimizing those.
Douglas Gentile, who runs the Media Research Lab at Iowa State University found that:
In the 1950s, the average American kid spent about 68 hours a week participating in sports, playing with friends, reading books, exploring the outdoors, or practicing a musical instrument.
By 2010, this had dropped to 14 hours a week (nearly 80% decrease)
Mothers are also only spending 2.5 hours per week (and fathers 30 minutes) interacting with their kids outside of normal family life interactions.
Gentile refers to this shift as The Displacement Effect: The more time we spend on distractions (like screens), the more that displaces other activities (like hobbies and interests).

Question: What is one distraction (screen-related or not) that is displacing time in your life that could be spent on other activities?

Q source: PRESENCE
Presence is more than being in the room — it’s being fully there.
In a world that constantly pulls at your attention, being mentally and emotionally available is one of the greatest gifts you can give the people closest to you. Your family and friends don’t just need your time; they need your focus. They need eye contact instead of a phone screen, listening instead of multitasking, empathy instead of distraction.
When you’re truly present, you communicate value. You signal, “You matter.” That builds trust, deepens connection, and creates the kind of relationships that actually sustain you long term. Success at work means very little if the people who matter most feel unseen.
Presence requires intention. It means setting boundaries with work, putting devices down, slowing your mind, and engaging with curiosity. It’s not always easy — especially for driven people — but it’s foundational.
At the end of the day, people won’t remember how busy you were. They’ll remember how you made them feel when they had your full attention.

Q-source: Presence - there's only so much of each of us to go around; how do we maximize our presence where it matters most?  
I think part of this begins with humility, particularly the humility to recognize that we are finite and that we have limitations about the number of things that we can handle. Our bandwidth is limited, and various things eat up that bandwidth, like work, chores, processing our own emotions, or even evaluating major decisions can use up some of our bandwidth in different ways. We need to be honest with ourselves about these things so that we can know when it is wise to say "no" in order to have bandwidth remaining for the people around us. 
Also had some good discussion about the importance of intentionally setting aside time to be present in each activity, both at work and with people. Along with saying “no” to some activities to preserve your bandwidth, presence also requires saying “no” to distractions or other tasks in the moment to stay engaged.

We all have different resources — money, talent, strength, experience — but there’s one thing we all get exactly the same amount of: 24 hours a day.
Time is the most limited resource there is. You can’t save it or get more of it. You can only spend it.
Everything in life competes for that time — work, family, friends, health, rest. That’s why Q-Source talks about Concentrica: prioritizing what’s closest.
Here’s the simple truth — your family is not replaceable. Your job is.
But it’s not just about priorities. It’s about presence.
When you’re at work, be at work. When you’re with your family, be with your family.
When we’re fully present, we don’t just spend time — we spend it well.

A man fights 3 battles.
1)  The first is internal, stripping away the conditioning, the comforting self deception, facing who he really is.  This is where most men quit as it requires vigorous honesty and discipline over comfort.

The internal struggle is real and our emotions and our ability to express them is, to me, part of being able to strip away the conditioning, at times to help regulate or level set the self deception, to be the real you.  With the Q-Source question of “Discuss the importance of being mentally and emotionally available in your relationships (particularly family and friends). I believe that the only way you can have the relation in relationship is to be mentally and emotionally available. Your family, your friends, your brothers in the gloom, sweat with you, grunt and groan and push yourselves and each other with you at each beatdown. And for some, this beatdown is therapy.  Working out aggressions and frustrations and complaints and pettiness and one’s one errors,and the impact of those errors on those who are important to you…can be therapeutic.  Doing something hard - together - creates a bond, a trust a belief in people whose hospital names you might not know.  And it’s that trust that enables, that supports, and hopefully fosters the atmosphere to share and be open, but also be available emotionally with those around us, so I hope we can be emotionally and mentally available for those outside of the gloom. But we also can’t run on full battery all of the time. We have to let ourselves replenish.  I would contend that one of the best ways to do that is to replenish  others.  Take a few seconds and drop a text or message.  Have a great day.  Hope your kids feel better soon.  Heard this comedy bit and wanted to share.  Listened to this podcast and it reminded of X. It’s those little things that can show you are a support, you are concerned, you want to be and are being a friend.  And when people know that, then when it’s time for something involving more mental and emotional strength, they know you can do that heavy lifting too.

Q SOURCE Mental Health - 
This topic is often challenging for men because many of us lack the familiarity of the language that surrounds mental health. We find comfort in keeping things simple and not thinking more deeply than we have to, thus not really seeking to understand our own mental health. But by refusing to grow in our mental health, we deny ourselves the ability to communicate effectively about our emotions with others, including our M’s and even our shorties. F3 nation has its own language that FNG’s are thrown into. Sometimes this language is off putting and strange enough to deter them from returning, but when that language is paired with understanding and friendly teaching, it becomes a special new aspect that actually makes FNG’s more welcome. All this to say, many men have had bad experiences trying to enter into understanding the world of mental health. Simply by offering other men a safe space, or letting our M’s know that we want to talk more about our mental health begins the process of familiarizing ourselves with this strange language that can ultimately make us more effective men and father’s for our communities. Counseling and therapy are ways to exercise and grow in using this language.

Men’s mental health awareness 

A lot of us men learned early that emotions are something to manage alone—or push down and keep moving. That works for a while… until it doesn’t. Scripture reminds us in Proverbs 20:5 that “the purposes of a man’s heart are deep waters,” and it takes wisdom to draw them out. Reconnecting with our emotions doesn’t mean becoming soft; it means becoming honest. The first step is naming what’s actually there. One word is enough—angry, tired, afraid, grateful. When we name it, we bring it into the light.

The second piece is brotherhood. Galatians 6:2 tells us to “carry each other’s burdens,” and that starts with listening, not fixing. Most men don’t need advice—they need permission. Permission to say, “I’m not okay today,” and still be welcomed. When we listen without judgment and show up consistently, we reflect Christ to one another. That’s what this ruck is about: carrying weight together—on the road and in life. No one here was meant to carry it alone.

Q-Source: “How can we help reconnect with our emotions as men if we’ve disconnected? How can we help others reconnect?”

I use the “learn one, do one, teach one” method. Start learning how to name your emotions and feel how they affect your body. Then bring that into conversations when it’s relevant instead of “stuffing it down.” Last, invite other guys to open up. If you ask, “How are you feeling?” and they say “Good,” respond with curiosity - “Really? What have you got going on that’s good right now?” While I suggested we don’t push people, we invite them, Babel correctly pointed out that it depends on your relationship. You’re allowed - encouraged even - to push your good friends to find out how they’re really doing. They might even need that, but you have to have an established relationship with them first to pull that off.

Men’s Mental Health Awareness 

A lot of men don’t struggle because they lack emotions—we struggle because we’ve trained ourselves to ignore them. One of the best ways back is through shared hardship. When we push our bodies together, we lower the defenses that keep everything bottled up. Pay attention to what shows up after the work is done—irritation, gratitude, pride, even heaviness. None of it is weakness; it’s information.

We help each other by creating safe space, not fixing or preaching. Ask real questions. Listen without trying to solve. Say “me too” instead of giving advice. Leadership starts with awareness, and awareness starts when we’re willing to notice what’s going on inside. That’s how stronger men—and stronger communities—are built.

Q Source: Adam Allred
A man fights 3 battles.
The first is internal, stripping away the conditioning, the comforting self deception, facing who he really is.  This is where most men quit as it requires vigorous honesty and discipline over comfort.
The internal struggle is real and our emotions and our ability to express them is, to me, part of being able to strip away the conditioning, at times to help regulate or level set the self deception, to be the real you.  With the Q-Source question of “How can we help ourselves or other men reconnect with their emotions when they struggle to do so?”  To me, the answer is founded in the idea of openness.  How open am I in sharing?  How open am I in listening/receiving?  If I’m open, how open?  How open are the receivers?  There needs to be a balance between the two, I think.  If there’s no balance, then either the speaker has overshared or the receiver just isn’t ready/equipped/knows how to respond.  It’s our job, I believe, to foster that environment SHOULD WE WANT THAT.  And if we don’t, we need to respect their choice while still creating an atmosphere of openness should a mind be changed.

Question for the Week:
How can we help ourselves or other men reconnect with their emotions when they struggle to do so?

A lot of men don’t avoid emotions because they don’t care — they avoid them because they were never taught how. Reconnection usually starts with the body, grows through safety, and sticks when we have words. As men, we help each other not by fixing or forcing, but by staying present, normalizing the struggle, and offering language until it becomes theirs. That’s leadership — and that’s brotherhood.

QSOURCE read between thangs:
1. Start With the Body, Not the Feelings
Point: Most men reconnect through their body before their words.
•	Emotions show up physically first:
•	Tight chest
•	Clenched jaw
•	Shallow breathing
•	Tense shoulders
•	Helping a man notice his body is often safer than asking, “How do you feel?”

Prompt to throw out:
👉 “What does stress feel like in your body?”

Why it works: It lowers defenses and builds awareness without pressure.

2. Normalize, Don’t Diagnose
Point: Men open up when they don’t feel analyzed or fixed.
	•	Instead of:
	•	“You should talk to someone”
	•	“You need to process that”
	•	Try:
	•	“That makes sense”
	•	“I’ve been there”
	•	“You’re not crazy for feeling that”

Prompt:
👉 “What’s something you’ve felt but thought you shouldn’t?”

Brotherhood before therapy. Presence, not solutions.

3. Borrow Language Until You Find Your Own
Point: Many men feel things clearly but lack words.
	•	It helps to offer language:
	•	“Sounds like frustration”
	•	“That feels like disappointment”
	•	Over time, men learn to name it themselves.

Prompt:
👉 “If you had to pick one word for your week, what is it?”

Leadership angle: Giving language is giving tools.

Question of the Week

What are some ways we can help our Ms and 2.0s with how they’re feeling?

⸻

Discussion Topics

1. Modeling Before Teaching

Topic: Our families learn emotional skills by watching us, not by our lectures.
	•	How do our Ms and 2.0s see us handle:
	•	Frustration
	•	Disappointment
	•	Stress after work
	•	Are we modeling regulation… or suppression/explosion?

Tie to mission: Leadership starts with example. You can’t outsource this.

⸻

2. Creating Emotional Safety at Home

Topic: Do the people in our house feel safe bringing emotions to us?
	•	What reactions shut our families down?
	•	Fixing too fast
	•	Minimizing
	•	Getting defensive
	•	What responses invite honesty?
	•	Listening first
	•	Naming feelings
	•	Staying calm

Connection to past discussion: Emotional strength = staying present, not shutting down.

⸻

3. Coaching, Not Controlling

Topic: Helping our Ms and 2.0s regulate instead of trying to manage their emotions for them.
	•	Difference between:
	•	“Stop crying”
	•	“I see you’re upset — what’s going on?”
	•	How can we guide without taking over?

F3 lens: We train leaders; we don’t micromanage.

⸻

4. Giving Language to Feelings

Topic: Most kids — and many adults — act out because they don’t have words.
	•	How often do we help them name emotions?
	•	“Sounds like you’re frustrated.”
	•	“That seems disappointing.”
	•	What happens when emotions are named instead of ignored?

Connection: Regulation starts with awareness.

⸻

5. Being Strong Enough to Stay Present

Topic: Can we stay engaged when emotions get uncomfortable?
	•	Which emotions are hardest for you to sit with?
	•	Tears?
	•	Anger?
	•	Fear?
•	What do you tend to do instead — withdraw, fix, distract?

Masculine framing: Strength isn’t escaping discomfort — it’s standing firm in it.

⸻

6. Repairing When We Miss It

Topic: What do we do after we get it wrong?
•	Do we:
	•	Apologize?
	•	Name our own emotions?
	•	Repair the relationship?
•	How does repair build trust more than perfection ever could?

Leadership truth: Credibility grows when men own mistakes.

⸻

7. Setting the Emotional Tone of the Home

Topic: Like it or not, dads set the emotional thermostat.
•	When we walk in the door:
•	Does tension rise or fall?
•	What small habits could shift the tone?
•	Pause before entering
•	Naming stress out loud
•	Intentional connection

Tie to mission: Strong homes build strong communities.

⸻
Challenge for the Week

Encourage each man to try one of these:
	•	Name an emotion you see in your M or 2.0 — without fixing it
	•	Stay calm through one emotional moment you’d normally avoid
	•	Repair one missed moment with honesty and ownership

Q Source: from Adam Allred
A man fights 3 battles.
1)	The first is internal, stripping away the conditioning, the comforting self deception, facing who he really is.  This is where most men quit as it requires vigorous honesty and discipline over comfort.
2)	The second is external, choosing a lan in a world of chaos, entropy and resistance.. and committing to it.  This battle involved building strength, competence and character while the world pushes back. 
3)	The third battle is collective, the rarest and most dangerous battle.  Speaking the truth against corruption.  Refusing to be owned, silenced or controlled.  A man who reaches this stage is seen as a threat to the status quo because he is no longer ownable, but a necessity for truth in society.  
To tie this to the question of the week…. Think about this…
If things are only good when I'm silent, then things aren't good at all.

That relates to that third battle, and it happens in the home. If your home is only happy when you're silent, you either need to go back to step 1 for some self-reflection, or "gird up your loins" i.e. put your big boy pants on - and get comfortable with making other people uncomfortable with the Truth.

And then the really BIG next step: apply that to your wife and kids. If your home is only happy because your wife says nothing, it's not happy. Same for the kids.

First, shoutout to D-20 for the great discussion material that he's been adding for our region. And as we have been discussing men's mental and emotional health, I hope we are allowing our conceptions of "manliness" to change as well. The concern is this: are we simply getting better at talking about our emotions and telling ourselves that it's okay to feel them while still holding to a lie that doing so is a sign of weakness or somehow makes us less "manly"? If our view of manliness doesn't change, then we sabotage ourselves, so allow me to push back with an example: King David. The man who fought Goliath, protected his sheep from bears and lions, led companies of men to success in battle, and reigned as a king is the same man who wept with his best friend when he was forced into exile, who danced with joy before God and before his subjects, who wrote many of the Psalms singing praise to God and also of his deep sorrows. He certainly made mistakes, but if we still have a hard time thinking that feeling is compatible with manliness, I hope that we can all reflect on and learn from David's example to know that they are indeed compatible.

Thang 3: Campfire and coffee
We sat around and contemplated ideas. Ideas like, what does it mean to be authentic? What do we gain out of being authentic with people? What's the cost of being authentic around people? If we come to the conclusion that being authentic is overall better for us and better for people around us, how do we draw the line between sharing and oversharing?

It was pure joy to me to sit around a fire and just listen to what everyone was saying. Authenticity builds trust, but risks being disliked. We can get comfortable with being disliked - look at men like Steve Jobs. He's polarizing; some people found him intense and energizing, while others found him abrasive, but whether you liked him or disliked him, everyone acknowledged his vision and creativity. We can also let people decide for themselves how much of us they are interested in. The next time someone asks how you're doing, give them an honest assessment and a rough sketch. Let them decide if they're curious enough to want more details. Ask for those details yourself - "tell me more about..." - and watch how people want to open up.

The people closest to you should get your best. Not everyone needs to know everything. It takes some effort and some perception and awareness of ourselves and our relationships to moderate ourselves (or not, when we're with the right people!) so that we can be both authentic and judicious - to be ourselves without "being a jerk about it" as one PAX put it.
