When it comes to relating to emotions, most of us were only taught two options  or “modes”— but there are really three: Controlled by, Controlling, and Regulating 

The goal is not to feel less.
The goal is to feel fully without losing leadership.

1. Being Controlled by Emotions
This is when:
•	Anger decides what you say
•	Fear decides what you avoid
•	Shame decides how you see yourself
•	Sadness pulls you into isolation
This looks like:
•	Yelling
•	Silent treatment
•	Emotional dumping
•	Impulsivity
•	Avoidance
The emotion is in the driver’s seat.
You aren’t weak — you’re just unregulated.

2. Controlling (Suppressing) Emotions
This is the “be a man” version many of us learned.
It looks like:
•	Not talking
•	Staying busy
•	Minimizing
•	Joking it off
•	“I’m good” when you’re not

The problem:
Suppressed emotions don’t disappear.
They come out as:
•	Irritability
•	Distance
•	Addictions
•	Explosions
•	Depression
You think you’re in control, but the emotions are just waiting for a crack.

3. Regulating Emotions (The Goal)
Regulation means:
I feel what I feel — but I choose how I act.
It’s the space between: Impulse → Response
Regulation looks like:
•	Naming what you feel
•	Slowing your body
•	Choosing words instead of reactions
•	Expressing emotions without attacking

A regulated man can say:
•	“I’m angry, but I’m not going to hurt you.”
•	“I’m overwhelmed, so I need a minute.”
•	“I’m sad, and I want to talk.”

That’s not weakness.
That’s strength under control.

Expressive Without Drowning People
This is critical for families.
There are two unhealthy extremes:
Silence & Flooding 
Silence is cold, detached and says “I don’t feel anything.”
Flooding is overwhelming, chaotic, and says “Here’s everything I feel all at once.”

Discussion Questions: 
        1.	Which mode did you grow up with — suppression or explosion?
	2.	Which do you default to under stress?
	3.	What would emotional regulation look like in your marriage or parenting?
	4.	What’s one emotion you avoid — and why?
	5.	What emotion do you feel the most but express the least?
(anger, fear, sadness, shame, disappointment, etc.)
	6.	When you’re stressed at home, do you tend to get louder, quieter, or busier? What does that do to the people around you?
	7.	What would it look like for your kids or your spouse to see you handle a hard emotion in a healthy way? What example are you currently setting — even unintentionally?

Q-Source: Men's Mental Health Awareness
How can we show up authentically, expressing emotion, while still remaining in the driver's seat?
The biggest struggle in my recent years has been parenting. Sure, a baby keeps you up at night and makes messes, but at some point you come to accept that it's just doing what babies do. Parenting toddlers and older kids has been a lot more challenging for me, especially when they realize the boundaries they can push with their words and actions.
I never really realized before now how much I want to try and control the situations around me, and when I have three little goobers under my care who seem very intent on pushing the buttons of everyone in their general vicinity, it makes it hard to model calm direction and still remain in the driver's seat of my emotions.
Going to some form of therapy is a stigma we as guys so often fight against, and yet it can be one of the most deepest sources of change in our lives. Every day, I'm trying to remember to show up emotionally for my family, and to force myself to pause before I react out of emotion.
We're so used to showing up for each other out in The Gloom, showing up to work as part of a team, or even showing up physically in our families, but how much of that time do we allow our emotions to also show up, in a healthy and intentional way? What does it look like to be in the driver's seat of your own heart?

Q-SOURCE:

How can we show up authentically, expressing emotion, while still remaining in the driver's seat?

1.)   The Next Conversation, by Jefferson Fisher discusses some aspects emotions have during our conversations.  During an argument a lot of emotions can be triggered.
a.)   Never try to win your next argument, talk to connect and understand the other persons position.
b.)   Each argument has two phases, ignition and cooling.  Ignition phase is caused by triggers.
c.)   Control Yourself:  Know your triggers…..
       (1)   Social triggers, “what will they think”
       (2)   Competence triggers, “if I fail am I not competent”
       (3)   Autonomy triggers, “Am I being micromanaged”
       (4)   Purpose triggers, “does my work matter”
       (5)   Value triggers, “are my beliefs disrespected”
       (6)   Loss triggers, “status or job”

   ***Recognizing your body’s ups and downs in the face of conflict gives you a huge
advantage, not only will you better understand your own reactions, you will also begin to identify the signs in the other person.

Q Source 
When it comes to relating to emotions, most of us were only taught two options  or “modes”— but there are really three: Controlled by, Controlling, and Regulating 

The goal is not to feel less.
The goal is to feel fully without losing leadership.

1. Being Controlled by Emotions
This is when:
•	Anger decides what you say
•	Fear decides what you avoid
•	Shame decides how you see yourself
•	Sadness pulls you into isolation
This looks like:
•	Yelling
•	Silent treatment
•	Emotional dumping
•	Impulsivity
•	Avoidance
The emotion is in the driver’s seat.
You aren’t weak — you’re just unregulated.

2. Controlling (Suppressing) Emotions
This is the “be a man” version many of us learned.
It looks like:
•	Not talking
•	Staying busy
•	Minimizing
•	Joking it off
•	“I’m good” when you’re not

The problem:
Suppressed emotions don’t disappear.
They come out as:
•	Irritability
•	Distance
•	Addictions
•	Explosions
•	Depression
You think you’re in control, but the emotions are just waiting for a crack.

Thing 2- Bear Complex Step-up ladder 
Each PAX carry a coupon to the picnic tables 
5 Bear Complex and 2 step up (2=1)
4 & 4
3 & 6
2 & 8
1 & 10

Rest  
1-3-1 ladder up 

Bear Complex- clean, front squat press, back squat

3. Regulating Emotions (The Goal)
Regulation means:
I feel what I feel — but I choose how I act.
It’s the space between: Impulse → Response
Regulation looks like:
•	Naming what you feel
•	Slowing your body
•	Choosing words instead of reactions
•	Expressing emotions without attacking

A regulated man can say:
•	“I’m angry, but I’m not going to hurt you.”
•	“I’m overwhelmed, so I need a minute.”
•	“I’m sad, and I want to talk.”

That’s not weakness.
That’s strength under control.

Expressive Without Drowning People
This is critical for families.
There are two unhealthy extremes:
Silence & Flooding 
Silence is cold, detached and says “I don’t feel anything.”
Flooding is overwhelming, chaotic, and says “Here’s everything I feel all at once.”

Healthy expression is:
Honest, measured, and owned
Instead of: “You make me so angry”
Say: “I’m feeling angry and I need to talk about it.”
Instead of: Dumping 10 emotions at once
Try: Naming 1 or 2 that matter most.

That’s how you share your inner world without drowning your wife or kids in it.

What This Means for Families
Your kids don’t need:
•	A stoic dad
•	Or an emotionally volatile dad
They need a regulated dad.
A father who:
•	Feels deeply
•	Speaks honestly
•	And stays grounded
That teaches kids:
•	Emotions are safe
•	People can be upset and still loving
•	Conflict doesn’t mean danger

That is how boys learn strength.
That is how girls learn what safety feels like.

Men’s Mental Health Awareness

What's the difference between feeling or regulating emotions and being controlled by them?

Feeling and regulating emotions means you notice what you’re feeling and stay in control of what you do next. You don’t ignore anger, stress, or frustration—you acknowledge it. But instead of reacting right away, you pause and choose a response that lines up with your values. Emotions become information, not orders.

Being controlled by emotions is when feelings run the show. Anger turns into sharp words, stress turns into poor decisions, and fear keeps you stuck. In those moments, the emotion feels urgent and powerful, and it pushes you to act before you think. That’s usually when regret shows up later.

The difference is simple: control versus control being taken from you. Strong men still feel deeply, but they don’t hand the wheel over to their emotions. They create a small pause, make a better choice, and move forward with intention—even when it’s hard.

Example:

You come home tired and stressed. The house is loud, your kids aren’t listening, and your wife asks you about something that needs to get done. The emotion you feel is frustration—and that’s normal.

Regulating that emotion looks like noticing it and slowing down. You take a breath and think, I’m overwhelmed, not angry at them. You lower your voice, give your kids a clear instruction instead of snapping, and tell your wife, “I need five minutes to reset, then I’m all in.” The feeling is real, but it doesn’t get to decide how you act.

Being controlled by the emotion looks like snapping at your kids or giving your wife a short, irritated response. Nothing gets solved, and now everyone feels tense. Same situation, same feeling—different outcome. One response builds trust and safety; the other teaches your family to brace for you.

Discussion question: What's the difference between feeling or regulating emotions and being controlled by them?

“Just because I’m angry doesn’t mean I’m right.” Emotions, especially anger, can have the same effect as alcohol or drugs and lower our inhibitions. I do and say things when I’m angry that I probably wouldn’t do when I’m calm. The same is true of fear, anxiety, and even excitement. It’s important for me to not intellectualize my emotions - to say “oh, I’m angry” but not let myself feel it. It’s equally important for me to pause, regulate myself when I’m feeling something strongly, and make sure the next thing I say or do isn’t the anger or fear acting through me. The Core Problem: Emotional Suppression
•Boys are often socialized to not show certain feelings — for example, being told not to cry, not to admit fear, or to “be a man.”  
•These messages usually come from well-meaning adults but invalidate boys’ real emotional experiences. 

How many of us heard versions of “boys don’t cry” growing up — and what did that actually teach us about emotional truths? “When boys are told they shouldn’t cry… we aren’t making them strong — we are teaching them to disconnect from themselves.”

Emotional Avoidance Has Real Costs

The article explains that when boys learn to distrust or ignore their emotions, those emotions don’t vanish — they go underground and show up in other ways, such as:
✔ Entering unsafe situations because fear is dismissed instead of heeded
✔ Difficulty recognizing and articulating needs
✔ Suppressing sadness until it becomes anger or risk-taking
✔ Challenges forming deep, healthy relationships

Emotions Are Strength — Not Weakness
The article reframes feelings as information, not liabilities:
	•	Fear alerts us to danger.
	•	Sadness signals loss and a need for connection.
	•	Anger highlights boundaries.
	•	Joy points toward meaning.

Toxic Masculinity’s Role
The piece links emotional suppression to broader cultural norms — often labeled toxic masculinity — where strength is equated with stoicism and dominance.

I would define “toxic masculinity” as masculinity that encourages aggressive and violent behavior and discourages emotion and self-control. In other words, masculinity that is both dangerous for women and harmful to men. It's crucial to note that toxic masculinity does not mean that all masculinity is toxic, but rather a dangerous type.

What Boys (and Men) Actually Need
Instead of dismissing feelings, the article advocates for emotion coaching — a research-based parenting approach that includes:
🟢 Noticing emotions
🟢 Validating them
🟢 Helping boys name what they feel
🟢 Teaching that emotions are safe, useful, and temporary

The Bigger Implication
If we continue teaching boys to disconnect from their inner world, we risk raising men who:
⚠ Don’t know what they feel
⚠ Don’t trust their own emotions
⚠ Struggle in relationships and self-understanding

Men’s Mental Health Awareness

What's the difference between feeling or regulating emotions and being controlled by them?

Feeling and regulating emotions means you notice what you’re feeling and stay in control of what you do next. You don’t ignore anger, stress, or frustration—you acknowledge it. But instead of reacting right away, you pause and choose a response that lines up with your values. Emotions become information, not orders.

Being controlled by emotions is when feelings run the show. Anger turns into sharp words, stress turns into poor decisions, and fear keeps you stuck. In those moments, the emotion feels urgent and powerful, and it pushes you to act before you think. That’s usually when regret shows up later.

The difference is simple: control versus control being taken from you. Strong men still feel deeply, but they don’t hand the wheel over to their emotions. They create a small pause, make a better choice, and move forward with intention—even when it’s hard.

Example:

You come home tired and stressed. The house is loud, your kids aren’t listening, and your wife asks you about something that needs to get done. The emotion you feel is frustration—and that’s normal.

Regulating that emotion looks like noticing it and slowing down. You take a breath and think, I’m overwhelmed, not angry at them. You lower your voice, give your kids a clear instruction instead of snapping, and tell your wife, “I need five minutes to reset, then I’m all in.” The feeling is real, but it doesn’t get to decide how you act.

Being controlled by the emotion looks like snapping at your kids or giving your wife a short, irritated response. Nothing gets solved, and now everyone feels tense. Same situation, same feeling—different outcome. One response builds trust and safety; the other teaches your family to brace for you.

Q Source (Shamelessly stolen from internet):

Comfort is the real enemy of progress because it quietly convinces you that where you are is good enough, even when you were meant for more. 

Here’s why comfort is dangerous: 

1. Comfort kills urgency - When life feels manageable, you stop asking hard questions. You delay growth because nothing is forcing you to move. 

2. Comfort weakens discipline - Growth requires discomfort—early mornings, rejection, learning, failing. Comfort chooses ease over effort every time. 

3. Comfort creates fear of change - You start protecting what you have instead of pursuing what you could become. Progress always demands risk. 

4. Comfort makes potential lazy - Talent doesn’t grow in convenience. Muscles, skills, faith, and character only develop under pressure. 

5. Comfort normalizes mediocrity - Once comfort settles in, average starts to feel acceptable. Dreams shrink to fit your routine. 

6. Comfort lies slowly - It doesn’t shout. It whispers: “Tomorrow is fine.” And tomorrow becomes years. 

Truth: Progress demands discomfort. Growth demands sacrifice. Becoming more requires leaving what feels safe.

I just passed 3 years in F3, and it’s been quite a ride that I didn't expect. I couldn't have imagined how integral to my life this community would become when Remax invited me to work out with him and some strangers in a park at an ungodly hour of the morning just over 3 years ago. But this community has become part of what keeps me anchored and pressing forward; the other men here encourage me to continue growing personally and helping me a bit more myself, to not be so overcome by fear that I hide behind a veil and let someone else take the reins, but rather to be comfortable with my own competence and grow still more by being willing to exercise that competence and potentially make mistakes in the process. Bad company corrupts good morals, and bad company is abundant, so I'm thankful to have been invited into another group filled with good company. But good company doesn't just happen - it is the result of the deliberate decisions and commitment on the part of each man here. We each strive to be better individually, and we make the decision to encourage our brothers to do the same and hold to their ideals too and to build them up rather than tear them down for the sake of our own egos. I am not yet where I want to be, and I never will be, but I am also not where I once was. The men of this region are a large part of that, so as this year closes and we head into the new year, let’s consider how to continue pressing on towards our goals of being better men and consider how to continue encouraging other men to do the same.

All of the requisite claims were claimed and disclaimers were disclaimed. No FNGs, so straight on to Warm-o-Rama. In celebration of the Fightin' Texas Aggie Women's Volleyball Team winning a national championship, all warm up exercises were done in cadence to a 12 count.

Next up, Reindeer Games!
With only 6 of us, there were quite enough to divide into 2 teams, so we were all in it together!

Game 1: Spades
1. Choose a "Rudolph" to lead your team
2. Four EMOM exercises.
3. Bid how many reps your team can finish of every exercise. If you bid 20, then you have 1 minute to do 20 reps of the first exercise, 1 minute to do 20 of the second exercise, and so on.
4. Both teams attempt the reps; if the team that won the bid finishes (every PAX completes every rep), they get a point. Otherwise, the other team gets the point.
5. Your team can help each other - if you finish your reps, take some for the man next to you so that you finish on time!

Since we were all on the same team, we didn't have a bidding phase.
First Rudolph was <band:refer user_key="AAARU4g9RYE-ED-iJVUxQHjz">Bareback</band:refer>, who started us with 15 reps of:

Game 2: Down the chimney
All the coupons were put in a pile. PAX lined up shoulder-to-shoulder in plank. The "presents" (coupons) were pulled through down to the other end one by one. Then Santa had to go back up the chimney with the empty bags, so back up the chimney with all the presents (cindy pull through the other direction with all the coupons.)

Game 3: Regifting
A fine holiday tradition where something isn't quite what you wanted, so you pass it along. Pile up the "presents" (coupons) and then line up single file. First PAX in line does a clean and press (deadlift into a thruster) to pick up a present, inspect it, hold it up to the "light", and then turns around and sets it down in front of the PAX behind him to "regift" it. Continue until all the coupons have been regifted. Reverse regifting was cut for time.

Game 4: Holiday storytelling
- Generosity and thankfulness are good traits for us to cultivate, as men. 
- Gratitude can help us overcome resentment, but good communication can help us prevent resentment.
- Don’t sweat the small stuff but advocate for yourself too. Be honest when you’re hurt and give other people the chance to be adults and be accountable.

Shaggy’s Sermon-

The Man Who Can’t Control His Reaction Will Lose Everything

Every man, at some point in his life, will face disrespect.
An insult.
A challenge.
A moment designed to provoke him.

But here’s the truth most men only learn after they’ve suffered the consequences:

It’s never the disrespect that destroys a man.
It’s his reaction to it.

Countless men—good men—have lost their marriages, their freedom, their careers, and even their lives because they reacted emotionally to a moment meant to test their discipline.

Not their strength.
Not their courage.
But their self-control.

---

1. Disrespect Hits Where Men Feel the Most Insecure

Disrespect doesn’t hurt because of the words.
It hurts because it exposes something inside you:

A wound.
A fear.
A doubt.
A place where your identity isn’t fully rooted.

That’s why insults feel personal—
they land exactly where you haven’t healed.

And when you don’t understand your insecurities,
your reactions become unpredictable, explosive, and costly.

---

2. Men Lose More From Reaction Than From the Original Offense

Many men aren’t in prison because they’re evil.
They’re there because they reacted too fast.

Many men didn’t lose their jobs because they were incompetent—
but because one moment triggered them.

Many fathers didn’t lose their children because they were uncaring—
but because they let anger speak louder than wisdom.

One moment of emotional weakness
can undo years of discipline.

That is the price of unchecked reactions.

---

3. A Man Who Can Be Provoked Can Be Controlled

When you’re easily triggered,
you’re easy to manipulate.

People learn:

* what tone gets under your skin
* what insult makes you explode
* what disrespect shuts down your logic

And once they learn what moves you,
they can move you anywhere.

Your emotions become the remote control
for other people’s intentions.

This is why emotional mastery
is not optional for men—
it’s survival.

---

4. Self-Mastery Makes Disrespect Powerless

When you confront your insecurities,
the insult loses its sting.

When you understand your triggers,
the enemy loses leverage.

When you discipline your emotions,
your response becomes a weapon
instead of a weakness.

A man who cannot be provoked
is a man who cannot be defeated.

His silence becomes strategy.
His calm becomes protection.
His restraint becomes power.

---

Final Word

Men, understand this:

It’s not the disrespect that defines you—
it’s the man you choose to be in the moment that follows.

Don’t get caught in emotional traps.
Don’t hand your power to people who want to see you break.
Don’t let a temporary offense create permanent consequences.

Be the man the moment requires—
not the man your emotions push you to become.

The man who can’t control his reaction
will lose everything.

But the man who masters himself
cannot be moved.

NOR-

🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄🎅🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄🎅🎄🎄🎄 

Warm-Up

We eased into the beatdown with the classics:
Side Straddle Hops – because nothing says “grown men in the dark” like synchronized jumping jacks.
Imperial Walkers – knee to elbow, looking like marching soldiers who lost the manual.
Michael Phelps – loosen the shoulders and pretend we’re all Olympic swimmers.
Little Baby Arm Circles – tiny circles, big humiliation.
Reverse Little Baby Arm Circles – because equality matters.
Concrete Ticklers / Grass Grabbers – depending on where you ended up standing.
High Knees – warm-up or early cardio punishment? Nobody knows.

The Workout – “Musical Coupons: F3 Edition”
PAX circled up with their coupon of choice, and YHC explained the rules.
-We rotate counterclockwise,
-We leave our coupon,
-We pick up someone else’s questionable life choice of a coupon,
-And we do their exercise — for 1:30 on, 35 seconds off.

Exercises chosen by our esteemed panel of fitness philosophers:
-YHC – Curls (of course)
-Narc – Bench Press (maybe he wanted to feel swole before sunrise)
Cobbler – Squats (the man loves pain)
Juice – Lunges (the worst)
O-Ring – Bent Over Rows (Classic)

Duck Duck Goose — F3 Style

This wasn’t your kindergarten version. This was the grown-man, sweat-dripping, regret-setting-in edition.
- We circled up in plank/push-up position (because why not?).
-One PAX jogs around tapping shoes: “Duck… duck… duck…”
-When you get a “duck,” you do a push-up.
-When a brother gets hit with GOOSE, all chaos breaks loose.
-Goose chases Duck around 4 columns while the circle cheers like we’re at a Roman arena.
- Loser: 10 squats in the middle.
-Everyone else: push-ups! 
It was beautiful, ridiculous, and surprisingly competitive…. Aaaaaand it’s a great way to stay in shape. (Family guy)

Next Up: The Track Lap of Truth
A casual trot around half the track to get warmed up for what’s next.


The Grand Finale: The 20-Meter Beep Test

We wrapped it up with the beep test, which basically says:

“Basically we’re gonna run until our legs give out or until the beeps get so fast you start hearing voices.”

Each round the beep gets 0.1 seconds faster, which feels like nothing at first… until suddenly you’re sprinting like a dad trying to catch a toddler running toward traffic.

PAX went back and forth scrimmage style, levels climbing until we gave up with trying to keep up to the stupid beeps! 

🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄
Men, this morning we pushed ourselves — but more importantly, we pushed each other.
The QSource says a team needs collective accountability the same way a HIM needs individual accountability. None of us accelerates alone. We all have blind spots, we all hit the Flux, and we all drift if there aren’t guardrails around us.

That’s why God gives us brothers.
Proverbs 27:17 says, ‘As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another.’
Iron doesn’t sharpen by being soft, it sharpens through contact, truth, and high standards.

A team without standards becomes static… but a team that holds each other accountable becomes dynamic, moving with purpose, protecting each other, and calling each other higher.

So today, remember this:
If you want to grow, don’t run from accountability, run toward the men who sharpen you.
And be that man for someone else.”
Ey!?

Wisdom helps us recognize that growth often hides inside challenges, that kindness carries farther than pride, and that every moment—whether joyful or painful—has something to teach.
To be wise is to live thoughtfully, choose purposefully, and move through the world with a deeper understanding of ourselves and others. Wisdom transforms knowledge into meaning, and everyday actions into something quietly extraordinary.

Effective organizations are not held together by the weight of their rules but by the strength of their relationships.
When rules replace genuine human connection, an organization slowly suffocates its own potential for movement and purpose.
The story of “Bob” at the gym shows how quickly a rule-bound culture can strip away the humanity required for trust and shared mission.
Organizations that rely on rules alone create compliant employees, but they never create leaders.
In contrast, Lizard-like organizations thrive because they minimize bureaucracy, maximize purpose, and release people to lead with initiative.
Such organizations are built through Dynamic Teams and Sua Sponte Leaders—men who take action not because they were told to, but because they know the mission matters.
As these teams grow, the Virtuous Leader stays just “43 Feet ahead,” guiding without controlling and empowering without micromanaging.
He understands that once a team surpasses twelve people, it must multiply rather than bloat, because movement—not institutional continuity—is the lifeblood of effectiveness.
Governance in a Lizard Organization points the way forward but never dictates the exact path, trusting the creativity and engagement of those doing the work.
Ultimately, the foundation of all virtuous leadership is love—the commitment to place others first and pursue purpose with humility, courage, and relational strength.

*Q Source: Equipping 
* Goo Nation would have us work to improve our weaknesses and get out of our Comfort Zones. 
* Equipping requires a man to Side Source weaknesses and focus his energy primarily on his strengths for the betterment of the Team.
* Doing (mostly) only what each man does best, the Members of a Team combine their actions into a potent and Dynamic cocktail of concerted effort.
* Know your role. If a man doesn’t know his role within the Team’s Mission, how can he possibly expect to perform it?
* The harder part of Teamwork is convincing a man to accept a role he doesn’t like or want but for which he is best suited within the Team. 
* It is inherent in our hard-wired ego to see ourselves in a certain way, despite the abundant evidence to the contrary.

Question of the Week: How could equipping and failure coincide and how does that make us better leaders?

People are pretty good at recognizing what they lack and seeking it in others. Or (even less intentionally) people will combine for reasons other than developing Teamwork, only then to recognize that they are more prosperous or effective as a team than they were as individuals.

Don't chase your Mission in isolation.
Lean in. Lock shields. Live Third.
B e c a u s e a m a n a l o n e c a n b e broken....

well... that's not easily defeated!

Q Source: Team Development 
* Because Community Membership is passive, requiring nothing more than general adherence to law and mores to be in good standing, a Community has no organic means with which to respond to urgent needs or external threat.
* Thus, it must depend upon Teams for the provision of security, the seeking of Advantage and the promotion of Shared Virtue.
* As a result, a Community without Dynamic Teams is at existential risk. Communities, as Groups that be, must be supported by Teams, the Groups that do.
* A Team cannot exercise Teamwork without strong Proximate relationships between its Members. Likewise, if a group is not Purposeful or has no Mission to fulfill, it is not a Team. It is a Club, which is only a loose combination of people seeking companionship.
* F3 uses the acronym TEAM to encapsulate the Team Development process the Virtuous Leader employs:
    * Trust
    * Equipping 
    * Accountability
    * Missionality
* Delegation: Authority can always be vested in others–but responsibility never can.
* The 80/1 Rule: the Q Delegates every Task that any man on his Team can do 80% as well as he can, except that 1% that absolutely and positively must be done by him.

Q source - TEAM:
F3 uses the acronym TEAM to encapsulate the Team Development process the Virtuous Leader employs:

T is for Trust: reliance between Team Members–the Virtuous Leader builds Trust.

E is for Equipping: matching the Team Members to its Mission–the Virtuous Leader ensures his Team has what it needs to be Effective.

A is for Accountability.TEAM: setting and maintaining high Standards within the Team–the Virtuous Leader instills a culture of Accountability within the Team that fosters Teamwork and mutual respect.

M is for Missionality.TEAM: prioritizing Team Mission accomplishment–the Virtuous Leader never lets the Team Members forget what they combined to accomplish.

For the Team to be Dynamic, the Virtuous Leader must continually reinforce each aspect of the process. He must constantly strengthen Trust, both between each Member and between the Members and himself. He must ensure that Team has the Members it needs to accomplish its Mission and that each man is fully Equipped to do what what is required of him for Team success. He does this by adding Members as needed, removing Members who cause the Team to Decelerate and realigning Members as they gain skills or the Team Mission changes. Finally, he must keep the the Mission forefront in all the Team does and continually direct and focus the Members toward its accomplishment.

Most importantly, the Virtuous Leader must place his own interests behind those of the Team and of each individual Member. He must Live Third. Doing so will cover a multitude of Leadership sins.

But if he fails to Live Third, nothing else he does do or doesn’t do will matter at all.

An Undesirable Outcome That Builds The Leadership Foundation
Failure is the crucible of the Leadership Development Process

So where does Failure fit into the Leadership development equation? What does it add to a man’s Leadership Foundation? If he already knows what a Virtuous Leader does and is–and is able is able to do and be those things himself–why must a Leader also Fail?

The reason is that Failure is a crucible. It is the forge by which a Leader is purified through the burning away of his me-first self-regarding nature. It matures him.

Mark 10
14 When they came back to the disciples, they saw a large crowd around them, and some scribes arguing with them. 15 Immediately, when the entire crowd saw Him, they were amazed and began running up to greet Him. 16 And He asked them, “What are you discussing with them?” 17 And one of the crowd answered Him, “Teacher, I brought You my son, possessed with a spirit which makes him mute; 18 and [k]whenever it seizes him, it [l]slams him to the ground and he foams at the mouth, and grinds his teeth and [m]stiffens out. I told Your disciples to cast it out, and they could not do it.”

28 When He came into the house, His disciples began questioning Him privately, “Why could we not drive it out?” 29 And He said to them, “This kind cannot come out by anything but prayer.”

– A Leader first learns this Leadership Principle during his Schooling where it becomes part of his head-knowledge

– During his Apprenticeship the developing Leader watches and helps his master pass praise/ take blame to see what it looks like when applied outside of the sterile classroom so that it will become heart-knowledge

– Finally, when given his Opportunity to Lead, he will put pass praise/take blame into Practice himself, outside of the protective bubble of the Apprenticeship where the Outcome is his sole responsibility

– But it will only be through Failure that the full responsibility for Outcome will crash down upon him when he bungles it by passing blame or taking praise (or both)

WHAT IS CHAD1000X?
CHAD1000X is a CrossFit Hero workout written in honor of Navy SEAL Senior Chief Chad Wilkinson, who died by suicide on Oct. 29, 2018 as a result of several traumatic brain injuries, blast-wave injuries, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) stemming from many deployments across more than two decades of service. Chad is survived by his spouse, Sara, a former CrossFit Seminar Staff flowmaster, and children, Kinsley and Hudson; as well as countless other friends and family.

The CrossFit community joins together annually on Veteran’s Day in thousands of CrossFit affiliates and garage gyms around the world to tackle this workout in Chad’s memory, raising funds to support Veteran Mental Health Initiatives through The Step Up Foundation, an organization Sara founded in Chad’s honor to change the narrative concerning the number of veteran suicides by dramatically expanding awareness regarding the effects of blast wave injury, traumatic brain injuries, and post-traumatic stress.

THE WORKOUT

1,000 box step-ups completed as a team, partner or individual for time.

3 OPTIONS:
1. Slick/Beginner // No rucksack. You pick the height of the step-ups.
2. Standard/Intermediate // 30#/20# rucksack. You pick the height of the step-ups.
3. Expert // 45# rucksack. Use 20″ box for step-ups.

WHY WE DO THE MURPH CHALLENGE
IN HONOR OF LT MICHAEL P. MURPHY

The Murph Challenge is not just a physical test, but also a mental and emotional one.
Participants are pushed to their limits and are encouraged to keep pushing through the pain and exhaustion, just as Lieutenant Murphy did during his final moments. The event is held annually on Memorial Day, and people from all over the world come together to honor Lieutenant Murphy and all those who have given their lives in service to our country. The Murph Challenge is a powerful reminder of the sacrifices made by our military and a testament to the strength and resilience of the human spirit. Never Forget.

The Murph workout goes as follows:
*   1-mile run
*   100 pull-ups
*   200 push-ups
*   300 air squats (bodyweight squats)
*   1-mile run

Modifications:  
1. Ditch the vest   
2. Break up your reps (I.e. 10 pull ups, 20 push ups, 30 squats x 10 rounds)
3. Modify Pull-ups to Cindy/Sandy rows

Everyone started in groups of two at the entrance of the court. Each group of two, staggered for space, ran one lap of the shorter of the tracks here at #therock. The Virtuous Leader makes himself dispensable
For those who are willing and able to tolerate the Hardship, the help-stage ultimately gives way to the do-stage. Here, the apprentice Leads alongside the master, encountering his own Problems and fashioning his own Solutions–but with the master close by to offer advice, counsel and Correction. It is in the do-stage that the apprentice first begins to Practice the positive tendencies that the master ingrained in him during the watch and help stages. Many, maybe most, of his initial Outcomes will be less than desirable. The master knows this because it was the same for him when he first began to do himself. Because he is a Virtuous Leader who seeks to Leave Right, the master rewards the apprentice’s Initiative and manages the Outcome, whatever it may be. The last two weeks we've been talking about Schooling and Apprenticeship. In Schooling the mentee gains knowledge. In Apprenticeship, they take their knowledge and hone it with the wisdom of the mentor. The next step in the LDP is Opportunity. This is where we thrust those we've been mentoring into their own leadership opportunities. Without those opportunities, those men will never get the chance to put everything they've learned into practice and gain the necessary experience to become effective leaders.

Opportunity is where the budding Leader takes on full responsibility for the success or failure of his efforts. He can no longer look to his mentor, but must now pass on all of the praise and fully shoulder the entirety of the blame.

Thang 3 (Floss’n)- The Gauntlet
Teams: Line up side-by-side in a plank position.
Equipment: Cindys/sandys stacked at one end of the line.
The Drill (Plank Cindy Pull-Through):
  - PAX hold a low Plank position (on hands or forearms).
  - The first PAX uses one arm to pull the Cindy stack under his body and then  passes it to the next PAX.
  - This continues down the line until all Cindys are at the opposite end.
  - Teams then reverse the process, pulling the Cindys back to the starting line.

Winner: Team Skillet

Teams: Line up side-by-side in a plank position.

Flapjack, repeat for all PAX in the opposite direction

Winner: Team Skillet

The Merkin Pyramid: Begin with 10x Merkins (Push-ups) and 1x Shoulder Taps (IC - Left + Right = 1 rep). Perform 10 Merkins, 1 Shoulder Tap; then 9 Merkins, 2 Shoulder Taps; all the way down to 1 Merkin, 10 Shoulder Taps.

Schooling is the first step in learning to be a strong, Virtuous Leader. It gives a man the basic knowledge and principles that apply to leadership in any situation—whether at work, in the community, or at home. These principles, like “Lead by Example,” never change, even though a good leader adjusts his approach based on who he’s leading and what the mission is.

A true leader connects what he believes with what he does. One key lesson is “Pass Praise and Take Blame,” meaning a leader gives credit to his team when things go well and takes responsibility when they don’t. This goes against human nature but earns trust and respect. Schooling teaches these ideas first in the mind so that, through experience, they become part of the heart.

Although Schooling starts the process, it never really ends. Like any skill, leadership grows through practice. The more a man leads, the more he realizes how much there still is to learn. A Virtuous Leader keeps learning and improving for life, always working to lead the right way and leave a lasting, positive impact.

One Cindy per pax. 

From table - start with half the Cindy’s. Stand side to side, facing opposite directions and twist to pass Cindy to next pax. Steady movement, focus on form. Last pax runs to the front of the line, continue passing until Cindy’s are at the field. Run back and repeat with second half of the Cindy’s. 

Plank Cindy pull through right across the field with first half of Cindy’s. Run back and start pull through left with second half of Cindy’s. Go to even with edge of sidewalk. 

Overhead Cindy carry around the sidewalk loop in the trees. 

Around the world carry to the basketball court. Switch directions halfway. 

With half of Cindy’s - American hammer Cindy pass right (Pass and last person moves to front of line) to mid court or three rotations of the line. Repeat with second half but left side. 

Curls for the girls while walking  to tennis courts.

Battle buddy up. Squat rocket over net to buddy. Step forward. Squat rocket back to first pax. Continue down net. When finished, go back to beginning, get second Cindy, switch sides of the net, and repeat process. Do both nets, full width of court. 

Zombie carry from tennis courts to volleyball pit. 

Murder bunny across volleyball pit. Bunny murder back. 

Salt shaker carry down to small pavillion and around back to big pavillion.

In F3, a Sua Sponte Leader is a man who has been freed to Lead. He is a Leader who exercises Individual Initiative (I2) by taking action in furtherance of his Group’s Articulated Purpose without specific instructions. He initiates Movement toward Advantage for his Group in the absence of explicit authority because he is that rare man who will Lead with or without another Leader to direct him. Q-Source and water break:
Q Source this week is on apprenticeship. The most important thing I took from it is the idea that good leadership isn’t hoarding knowledge and making all of the decisions. Good leadership is making yourself completely dispensable. Lead your way out of your current job so that you can move on to the next calling. I watch the leadership at the company I work for doing this. It’s impressive to see men and women constantly finding people to take on roles that they once held, until they’re nothing but advisors. They retire knowing that they’ve transferred their positive habits to the next generation.

As fathers, I can’t emphasize the importance of this enough. My oldest daughter turns 17 in February, 18 in just a year after that. She’ll be off and mostly on her own (with help as needed) but I’m confident that I won’t need to do much beyond offer the occasional bit of advice. She’ll be ready to do the job far better than I was at that age.

So what would you change in your life, right now, to make use of apprenticeship, either as a learner or a mentor?

From the discussion this morning, YHC resolves to do better at delegating tasks to give others the opportunity to learn what he's doing, even if it means it takes longer and I have to fix mistakes. That's how we all learn, and that also teaches me patience.

In the Q3.12, it reads, “Courage is not the absence of fear. There is no such thing. All sane human beings have a fear mechanism that is alive and kicking at all times. Whether one believes it to be the product of devine design or random evolution, our built-in fear mechanism is what keeps us alive long enough to participate in the creation of new human beings. 

Without fear, we would incessantly and ignorantly blunder into harm’s way with deadly consequences. Without fear, the human race would have long ago ceased to exist.
The same could be said of our inborn desire to procreate. Without the sex-drive, the continued existence of the human race would be unlikely. Yet, this instinct to copulate is not intended to rule over us. If not tempered by Virtue, the sex-drive grows into a lust that is inimical to the harmony and health of the Group.

Fear untempered is just as deadly. To give over completely to one’s instinct to avoid danger, regardless of the consequences, is the opposite of Courage. It is cowardice. If we were all to flea from danger all the time, the Community would be slowly devoured, starting with the slowest man and ending with the fastest. No one would be safe.

Courage begins with the recognition that while peace should always be our goal there are some threats that confront the Community that simply must be fought. The Virtuous Leader is able to set aside his fear of danger sufficiently that he can Influence other men to fight with him rather than flee when such threats arise. As with the tempering of all human instincts, the ability to set aside fear is a Virtue borne of training. We may be born to run, but we must be taught to fight. Thus, the ethos of Courage is passed from Leader to Leader through the process of Positive Habit Transfer.

Discretion is a cage with velvet bars. I don’t get up in the morning and decide whether to exercise that day. Because my Habits are so ingrained, I just find myself at a Workout every morning via a series of non-decisions that were easy to make because I didn’t have make them. By abandoning discretion to Habit, I have freed myself from having to decide.

Second, the more reliable I am in the small things, the more people will believe they can rely upon in me in the big things.

Habits (bricks) form routines. 

Guardrails protect a man from the Flux, which is his emotional reaction to the peaks and valleys that appear with regularity throughout his life. It is that feeling of “backsliding” or “going through a rough patch” that we all periodically encounter. Because he is Consistent, the Virtuous Leader may appear to his followers to be immune from the Flux, but in truth his steadiness is only the fruit of his Preparedness.

Flux will happen - routine / guardrails helps you overcome it. 

How can a man learn to be Consistent?

Hebrews 13:8, which says, "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever".

15 minute discussion:

1. Setting the Stage (2 minutes)

This week we’re looking at commitment through the lens of simplicity. The Q Source reminds us: Simplicity is the foundation of Consistency. If we want to stay committed long-term, we have to cut the clutter and focus on what really matters.

⸻

2. First Reflection Question (3-4min) the convo was so good we kept it going til time.
What’s one area of your life where clutter—mental, physical, or schedule—gets in the way of consistency with what matters most?



Nuggets from conversation:
-habits like close out rituals at work promote being present with your family
-mental clutter prevents us from seeing the goals clearly
-habit building is a big building block to staying consistent and simplifying our environment to be successful
-commitment and consistency build on each other. by committing to an action or belief system you can create habits that promote being consistent

⸻

3. Digging Deeper (3–4 minutes)
• Ask: “When we make life more complicated than it needs to be, what usually suffers first—our commitments, our relationships, or ourselves?”
• Draw out responses that highlight the cost of complexity (stress, missed priorities, burnout).

⸻

4. Personal Practice & Leadership (3–4 minutes)
• “What’s a simple, repeatable habit that helps you stay committed even when life gets messy?”
• Follow-up if time: “How can our own commitment to simplicity set the tone for our family, team, or shield lock?”

⸻

5. Wrap-Up & Takeaway (1–2 minutes)

Homework: Find one thing you can simplify this week—something you control—that will help you show up more consistently where you’re most needed?

Simplicity isn’t about doing less—it’s about removing what doesn’t matter so we can stay consistent with what does. That’s how we keep our commitments strong.”

WHY WE DO THE MURPH CHALLENGE
IN HONOR OF LT MICHAEL P. MURPHY

The Murph Challenge is not just a physical test, but also a mental and emotional one.
Participants are pushed to their limits and are encouraged to keep pushing through the pain and exhaustion, just as Lieutenant Murphy did during his final moments. The event is held annually on Memorial Day, and people from all over the world come together to honor Lieutenant Murphy and all those who have given their lives in service to our country. The Murph Challenge is a powerful reminder of the sacrifices made by our military and a testament to the strength and resilience of the human spirit. Never Forget.

The Murph workout goes as follows:
*   1-mile run
*   100 pull-ups
*   200 push-ups
*   300 air squats (bodyweight squats)
*   1-mile run

Q source 
Candor, the first of F3’s Leadership Virtues, is the practice of both graciously telling and willingly hearing hard truths. Unlike Leadership Skills (Vision, Articulation, Persuasion, Exhortation), which make a leader effective, Leadership Virtues shape his moral character and determine whether he is truly virtuous.
Nature of Truth and Candor
	•	Truth is immutable—unchanging over time—and can be universal (applies to all) or particularized (applies to individuals or small groups).
	•	Easy truths (good news) require no virtue to tell. Hard truths (painful or disruptive news) demand candor because they cause discomfort.
Why Hard Truth Matters
	•	Virtuous Leaders tell hard truths because withholding them erodes trust.
	•	Effective but un-virtuous leaders hide truth under the guise of protection, but deceit breeds long-term distrust and eventual failure.
	•	Candor creates trust, and trust fuels a group’s resolve to endure hardship together.

Two-Way Street of Candor
	•	Virtuous Leaders must both tell hard truths and be able to hear them.
	•	To hear truth, a leader must demonstrate emotional discipline and stability, creating an environment where others feel safe to speak honestly.
	•	Passive approaches (like “open-door” policies) are insufficient; leaders must actively seek truth and handle it maturely.
Graciousness in Candor
	•	The “gracious” element lies in how a leader receives bad news—with equanimity, humility, and focus on outcomes rather than ego.
	•	Leaders who overreact discourage honesty; leaders who handle truth calmly foster trust and shared responsibility.
	•	By modeling candor, leaders teach others to think before acting, explain their reasoning, and embrace shared accountability.
Lasting Impact
	•	Without candor, influence may be temporary, but trust will erode.
	•	With candor, leaders establish a durable bond of trust and love with their followers, enabling resilience through hardship and chaos.

The Q-source this week is on Candor - graciously telling the hard truth and demanding to hear it from others. After some recent conversations, I've been thinking about a related but slightly different matter: the courage to speak one's mind. It reminded me of Ralph Waldo Emerson's essay, "Self Reliance," which I read some time ago but is essentially about this idea.  
"It is easy in the world to live after the world's opinion; it is easy in solitude to live after our own; but the great man is he who in the midst of the crowd keeps with perfect sweetness the independence of solitude."  
"Familiar as the voice of the mind is to each, the highest merit we ascribe to Moses, Plato, and Milton is, that they set at naught books and traditions, and spoke not what men but what they thought. A man should learn to detect and watch that gleam of light which flashes across his mind from within, more than the lustre of the firmament of bards and sages. Yet he dismisses without notice his thought, because it is his. In every work of genius we recognize our own rejected thoughts: they come back to us with a certain alienated majesty. Great works of art have no more affecting lesson for us than this. They teach us to abide by our spontaneous impression with good-humored inflexibility then most when the whole cry of voices is on the other side. Else, tomorrow a stranger will say with masterly good sense precisely what we have thought and felt all the time, and we shall be forced to take with shame our own opinion from another."  
Let’s be bold in speaking up when we think everyone else is thinking the same thing. And even if others aren’t thinking the same thing, let’s still be bold to speak our minds (graciously) and share the boldness of those who wrote down their thoughts for others to read and ponder, and maybe even criticize.

Candor is the first Leadership Virtue, and it means both telling and hearing the hard Truth with grace.

Truth never changes—it was true yesterday, it is true today, and it will be true forever.

Some Truths are universal, like the need for water, while others are particular, like a man’s struggle with addiction.

Easy Truths, like good news, require no character to share; anyone can do that.

Hard Truths cause pain and disruption, which is why only a Virtuous Leader has the strength of character to tell them.

A leader who withholds the hard Truth in the name of “protection” is really deceiving, and deceit always destroys trust.

Trust is the fuel that gives men the courage to leave comfort and endure pain in pursuit of Advantage.

Without Candor, any success a leader has will be temporary, because lies always surface and erode trust.

Candor is a two-way street: leaders must also be willing to hear the hard Truth without anger or defensiveness.

This requires emotional discipline, humility, and a servant’s heart, focusing on the Group rather than personal comfort.

Leaders must actively seek the Truth from their people, asking hard questions about what they did and why.

When a leader graciously receives the hard Truth, it builds deep trust, strengthens shared leadership, and allows the Group to endure hardship together.

Men, today I want to talk about Candor—the first of the F3 Leadership Virtues. Candor is simply this: graciously telling the hard Truth, and being willing to hear it yourself.The easy Truths don’t require character. Anyone can tell you that your flight is on time or that you got a promotion. But when the Truth brings pain or disruption—like telling someone they’ve failed, or that their choices are destructive—that takes strength of character. That’s what Candor demands.A leader who hides the hard Truth in the name of “protection” is really just lying. And lies always destroy trust. Trust is the fuel that gives men the courage to step into pain and chaos in pursuit of a better future. Without Candor, a leader may succeed for a while, but eventually the truth comes out, and his leadership crumbles.Candor is also a two-way street. It’s not just telling the Truth—it’s being willing to hear it yourself. A Virtuous Leader takes hard news like a pro, without flipping out, because he knows it’s not about him—it’s about the mission and the team.


Here’s the bargain of Candor: a leader loves his men too much to lie to them, and they trust him enough to believe him. That bond, built on Truth, is what allows a group to endure hardship and move forward together.

THA THANG.
Inspired by Billy Madison's journey back through school, this BD featured a test of 12 reps followed by a mosey up the tower. For each new grade level, we would perform a new exercise followed by each previous grade level's exercise... each round topped off with a trip up the stairs to that grade level. As we moved up in grade level, it got increasingly harder.

Due to the height of the tower, the goal was to get a "Navasota diploma" (shoutout <band:refer user_key="AABEW9UQKLuXQWY-q2Q1kBuT">Mario</band:refer> and <band:refer user_key="AADoz4MGU5jtw3g2cGonIkhF">Jake</band:refer>), or to finish 9th grade. Here's what it looked like for each grade (and rep totals):

Kindergarten-SSH (90 total)
1st grade-  Merkins OQ (78 total)
2nd grade- LBC (66 total)
3rd grade- Squats (54 total)
4th grade- Carolina Dry Docks (42 total)
5th grade-  Flutter Kicks IC (30 total)
6th grade-  Calf Raises OYO (18 total)
7th grade-  Shoulder Taps (6 total)
8th grade-  American Hammers OQ (6 total)
9th grade-  Burpees OQ (6 total)

Despite mumble chatter threats to drop out and calls for "nap time" and "spring breaks", the PAX did honorably. In a crunch for time, after 6th grade, YHC audibled to skip 7th and 8th (because the HIM are exceptional) and finish with 9th grade and a mosey all the way to the top of the tower. The PAX dominated it and earned their diplomas. To sum up the workout:

"This BD was one of the most insanely idiotic things we have ever done. At no point in our rambling, incoherent mumble chatter were we even close to anything that could be considered a rational thought. Everyone in the PAX is now dumber for having done it. We were awarded no points, and may God have mercy on our souls."

WARREN MOON - The Playmaker 🌔
“My legacy isn't about what I did playing football, but how I use the opportunities that came from playing football.”

“I was always geared towards either wanting to finish number one or be number one as far as the best player that I could be, or be the best player at my position in the league. I wanted that to be a constant reminder to my teammates that they looked to their leader who is wearing that number, this is what you should strive for as well.”

“My legacy isn't about what I did playing football, but how I use the opportunities that came from playing football.”


*Born on November 18, 1956, in Los Angeles, Moon was the middle child amongst six sisters. His father, Harold, was a laborer and died of liver disease when Moon was seven years old. His mother, Pat, was a nurse, and Warren learned to cook, sew, iron, and housekeep to help take care of the family. Early on, Moon decided that he could play only one sport in high school because he had to work for the rest of the year to help his family. Moon chose to play football as a quarterback since he found that he could throw a football longer, harder, and straighter than anyone he knew.[4][5][6][7][8]

*Moon enrolled at Alexander Hamilton High School, using the address of one of his mother's friends to gain the advantages of a better academic and athletic reputation than his neighborhood high school could offer. Moon had little playing time until his junior year, when he took over as the varsity starting quarterback. As a senior in 1973, Moon was named to the all-city team and the football team reached the city playoffs

Moon attended two-year community college  West Los Angeles Collegeand was a record-setting quarterback as a freshman in 1974

Moon played college football for the Washington Huskies, where he was named Pac-8 Co-Player of the Year in 1977 and was MVP of the Rose Bowl the following year upsetting Michigan. Due to not generating interest from NFL teams, he began his professional Canadian Football career with the Eskimos in 1978.

In 1982, Moon became the first professional quarterback to pass for 5,000 yards in a season

Moon played six seasons with CFL before being 28 and going to the NFL Houston Oilers.


* First African-American Hall of Fame QB: In 2006, Moon became the first African-American quarterback inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. His perseverance and excellence opened doors for subsequent generations of black quarterbacks. 

* A legend in two leagues: Moon is the only player to be inducted into both the Pro Football Hall of Fame and the Canadian Football Hall of Fame.

Brothers, Persuasion is the third F3 leadership skill. It’s the ability to move men toward a better future—even when they resist, because leaving the status quo feels uncomfortable.
True leadership doesn’t come through force or trickery. That’s the way of tyrants, and it never lasts. Real Movement must be voluntary, sparked by trust and influence.
The biggest obstacle we face is inertia—what F3 calls the Crack Pipe of Mañana. Men nod their heads, say “that’s a great idea,” and then put it off for tomorrow. Paul himself saw this when people liked his message but delayed action.
The key to Persuasion is starting small. Don’t demand full agreement or overnight transformation. Instead, get a man to take one step—a little Movement. Small steps create momentum, and momentum changes lives.
That’s why F3 works. We don’t try to argue a guy into believing in male leadership or community change. We just ask, “Want to get in better shape? Come try a free workout.” One small step leads to big Movement.
Leaders persuade upward by serving and encouraging, not downward by controlling. Our job is to pull the Crack Pipe of Mañana out of our brother’s mouth and invite him to take that first step toward Advantage.

“To tell you the truth, I thought I would be returning kicks and punts my whole career. I thought that was going to be my deal, and I was fine with that.”

“If you're willing to put yourself and your dreams on the line, at the very least you'll discover an inner strength you may not have known existed.”

“The road to our dreams has many detours. I never doubted myself.”

Bears Scout Greg Gabriel on draft night - 
“He is going to scare other teams. He's great with the ball in his hands. He's very, very dangerous, real fast."

“Things happen in NFL games. I don’t try to dwell on it. I try to say, It happened. Let’s move onto the next one.”

*Grew up pretty rough life, mom had him his bother in 10th grade and was pregnant with him in 12th. Dad died when he was 14 and had to lean on his mother, step father and coaches for support and guidance. 
*Very talented in High school and earned the right to go to Miami Hurricanes 
*In college he befriended his idol Deion Sanders through a Hurrican connection Ed Reed… Deion became his mentor and got the name “anytime”. He was a strong mentor through entire career.  
*Played college ball for Miami Hurricanes - only player in recent years to play Office, Def & ST
*He always struggled to find his place. 

*Drafted as a corner back but after first year quickly switched to return man and wide receiver
*Had a great relationship with his coach Lovie Smith that helped him find his true potential 
*11 Seasons in the NFL and is also the only player to return the opening kick of a Super Bowl for a touchdown… as a rookie!
*He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2024, becoming the first player inducted primarily as a return specialist.
*Devin Hester Rule, kickoff from 35 instead of 30
*During his HOF speech, he gave thanks to God and the people around him that guided him down the path to finding his place.

“Nobody wanted me. Scouts told me to go to school, to forget baseball. Coaches said, 'You're never going to make it.' I appreciated their honesty, because I think when someone tells you something you may not like, you have to use that as fuel for motivation.”

“A pitcher never gets me out. I get myself out. That's no disrespect to the pitcher, but there should be no excuse for failure. You can't have an excuse to fail.”

“I was a last round draft pick. Nobody wanted me. I could count the amount of scouts that told me to go to school, to forget baseball.”

*Growing up, Mike was always in love with baseball. His father was well connected being in the car business and had Ted Williams see him bat in his back yard when he was only 16 years old. 🤯 

*Went to college at Unv of Miami… rode bench entire first year…. Transferred to Miami Dade community college and did really well but still got zero attention from any scouts… terrible scouting reports. 

*62nd Round Draft pick in 1988… 1,390th pick
*Piazzas father and Tommy LaSorta grew up together and Mike was drafted as a favor as long as he moved positions from 1B to Catcher.
*Seriously struggled in the minors where he briefly quit the game…played winter ball in Mexico to develop his catching skills… played against current MLB players… 
*Moved up to majors after four years and the rest is history…

*He caught two no-hitters during his time with the Los Angeles Dodgers: one by Hideo Nomo and another by Ramón Martínez

*Last catcher at Shae Stadium with the Mets

*He played in the first Baseball game in NY after 9/11…. Braves vs Mets…. He hit a bomb late in the 8th inning to clinch the game… very emotional and significant moment for New Yorkers… that jersey later sold at auction for over $300k…

*He is the best power-hitting catcher in MLB history and probably the best offensive catcher, period… than Johnny Bench, Carlton Fisk, Thurman Munson, Pudge, Yogi….

The concept of an Articulated Purpose involves clearly communicating a visualized end-state that significantly differs from the current status quo, requiring collective action to achieve it. A Virtuous Leader inspires others to join this movement by articulating a compelling vision that is easily understood and memorable, igniting a desire for action. Articulation is a distinct skill from visualization, and while everyone can articulate, many choose not to due to self-doubt or fear of rejection. These obstacles—initial lack of skill and resistance to change—can be overcome through persistent practice, as demonstrated by the F3 organization's iterative improvement in articulating its mission to invigorate male community leadership. Failure, such as a poorly executed first attempt (Virgin-Q), is a critical part of the learning process, building a foundation for leadership growth through repeated effort. Articulation prioritizes understanding over acceptance, as people naturally resist change due to fear of pain and chaos. A leader’s role is to ensure clarity of the vision, accepting that initial resistance is normal, and focus on persuading followers once they comprehend the goal.

I was reflecting on my 2 years of F3 and considering posting some thoughts/takeaways, etc but am hesitant because it’s definitely not about me. I think back to the awesome message <band:refer user_key="AAAwjVK_Yu2V9tQtVcao2xAM">Dodgeball</band:refer> shared on his 1 year anniversary and how it reinvigorated me to stick with F3 at a tough time (for anyone that has not read it - or hasn’t read it in a while, go check it out - it’s incredible: https://band.us/band/87102273/post/3235 
So with that in mind, I’ll share my thoughts (not that they will be anywhere close to as inspiring as Dodgeball’s but just in the off chance that one of you Pax out there needs to hear this). 

Two years ago, on August 3rd, 2023, I showed up to The Keep for the very first time. Honestly, the only reason I came out was because Thunderbird texted me a couple of times about the Keep Launch and then he texted me again after it. I figured the only way to get him off my back was to show up once, make a fool of myself, and then tell him F3 wasn’t for me.

So I walked over—no water, no gloves, no idea what I was walking into. The workout was a 30-30. Looking back, it was a pretty standard beatdown probably not all that challenging (no offense @Dr. Frasier Crane), but at the time, it was the most exercise I’d done in probably 20 years. I had to sit out halfway through just to keep from falling out. I left that morning unsure of WTF I had just experienced. Still, I felt proud of myself for showing up and I remember that day going back and forth on whether I’d go back the next day. I ultimately decided to show up again and the rest is history. 

Had I not, I would have missed out on so many things I’ve learned about myself in 2 year, among those are 
* I can run a whole mile without stopping.
* I’m now the kind of guys that has half a garage full of sandbags, weight plates and 100 other fitness related things I never would have imagined owning.
* I did the Chad 1000X Step-Up Challenge (unweighted) only three weeks after a nasty ankle sprain.  I planned to just to watch. Then I figured I’d try 100. Then maybe 500. Somehow, I ended up doing all 1,000 — balancing every step-down on my good ankle. That day proved to me that I could do way more than I thought possible.
* I did 10,000 merkins in 100 days
* I found my creativity again. F3 gave me an outlet to start making AI images and memes. Not much opportunity to be creative as an attorney so I hadn’t had a chance to use that part of my brain years. It’s reminded me how much joy it brings to create and share and I’ve leaned into.
* I climbed 110 flights of stairs for 9/11 Memorial Stair Climb last year.
* I did the Christmas Ruck almost 10 miles with weight, and remembered I can plan a pretty epic after party.
* I’ve done the 1776 Challenge twice (this year with a weight vest).
* Last September, I did every week of Iron Pax Challenge after thinking all the guys doing the IPC in 2023 were way beyond any fitness level I would ever achieve. Looking forward to crushing that again next month.
* I proved to myself that I can manage a semi-reasonable diet and I know have the discipline needed to cut out crap foods when I want to.
* I’ve made friends with tons of awesome dudes. Not even going to try to call out anyone because I would forget someone but you guys mean a lot to me. Honestly before F3, I was done with friends. I had no interest in expanding my social networks and in fact I was pretty much over dealing with other people in general. I was bitter and pessimistic and I saw the worst in everyone. 

These things stand out as a memories because they were hard. They forced me out of my comfort zone and into an area I hadn’t lived in quite a while.  F3 made that possible. Sometimes I hear you guys say things like, “you do so much for F3, don’t get burned out” but the truth is, I get far more out of F3 than I ever put in. These two years have made me a better man, a better husband, and a better father. And I owe that to you men who show up in the gloom day after day.

If you haven’t read Freed to Lead yet—do it. If you’ve read it, go back and put it into practice. F3 doesn’t need spectators. We need your talents, your energy, your ideas, and your willingness to lead. This isn’t a spectator sport. You don’t have to wait for permission to do something that makes the region better. If you see a need, fill it. If you’ve got a fire in you to lead, step into the role. Even if you’re not sure you have what it takes, what have you got to lose? It’s a free men’s workout group. The stakes are pretty low, but the gains are priceless. The more you give to F3, the more F3 gives back—not just to you, but to all of us.

It’s been an awesome 2 years for me personally and for F3Aggieland as a whole. Theres been a whole lot of 1% improvement, but there is a whole lot more to come. Looking forward to continuing the ride with all of you. 

We’ve come a long way. But the best is still ahead, on to the next 43 feet.

-Willie Mays was a lifetime .301 hitter in the big leagues… Tony Gwynn was as a lifetime .302 hitter with two strikes…

Trust is essential between Parents and 2.0’s … Trust is when you listen and obey, even when you don’t understand things fully. A leader’s job is to make a decision and guide a group in a certain direction, project or adventure. Trust involves believing someone when they say they will do something. Trust means trying not to hurt someone else. Trust, like a bridge, can be broken when someone gets hurt - through a mean word, a broken promise, or when you expected someone to help you when you were hurting or alone. Trust is friendship. It’s built by asking questions, and by sharing personal things - your ideas, your emotions, what you would like to do, and helping each other out. It also means asking others about what’s going on in their lives - like when you see a new kid sitting alone at school who might be lonely, and going to ask them what they enjoy. Trust is also faith. It’s believing the best about someone, choosing to forgive them if they hurt you, and trying to understand people & what their motivations or pressures are.
How do you build trust? How can trust be broken? Do you have examples?

Q-source: Trust  
Trust takes time to build, but it can be very quickly lost. In general, conferring trust upon someone else requires a good track record to demonstrate why that trust is warranted. And, as the Q-source points out, the track record can't be based on simple things - it requires stress testing, allowing ourselves or someone else to go through difficult situations to prove that we or they are capable of bearing the burden of larger responsibilities, thereby demonstrating that trust is warranted. In one sense, this is another instance of the principle "he who is faithful with little will be faithful much" - with an increasing number of stress tests, or with tests of increasing stress, a man can demonstrate that they can be trusted with more. But, here's a question I want each of us to consider: am I keeping a record of the history of my stress tests? This is related to the faith component because, along with demonstrating the kinds of things we have been prepared for and therefore what others can trust us with (along with where we should be able to trust ourselves), such a record is also a testament to the trustworthiness of our Creator. I try to journal, and while I don't do so on a regular basis, even sporadic journaling has still left me with many recorded instances of why I can trust my God and what he has prepared me for.

Ten days ago, my grandfather Denton Basset passed away at the age of 95.

Today would have been his 96th birthday.

He had this amazing ability to turn hardship into something joyful. When Guillain-Barré syndrome slowly bound him to a wheelchair, my son JP remembers how Poppy made it fun, giving him rides down the long driveway in his motorized scooter, with JP riding in his lap or being pulled behind in a wagon. The scooter wasn't a symbol of his limitations. It became a vehicle for adventure, joy, and connection with his great-grandkids.

My grandfather was a hospital chaplain for most of his career and, it seemed, for most of his retirement as well. Over the years, various family members had a few visits to the hospital . When my grandparents would come visit whoever it was, Grandma would typically enter the room alone. We'd all ask "Where's Grandpa?". And without fail, the answer was: On the way up he had always found someone in another room who also needed his comfort.

Even during many of his own hospital stays, he could never quite switch off chaplain-mode. He never met a stranger. He always wanted to meet you, pray with you, and make sure you knew you were loved, by him and by God.

He was a man of deep faith, bottomless patience, quiet strength, and a sharp sense of humor. He taught my how to work hard, how to care for others, how to see the good in everything, and how to make even the smallest moment feel like it mattered.

I will miss him deeply.

Another AOlympics is in the books!

30 HIM from 5 different F3 Aggieland AOs met on the field of CSMS for a chance to earn eternal glory for their home AO.

(The list of participants is at the end of the post for readability)


The Benchmark
Every HIM in attendance completed the F3 Aggieland Quarterly Benchmark with the top 5 finishers in each event earning points for their respective AO.

The Relay
Following completion of the Benchmark, 4-man teams from each AO assembled on the track for a medley relay consisting of the following legs:
100m bear crawl
200m farmer carry
300m 80lb sandbag carry
400m AO flag run

The Herculeans
In keeping with tradition, each AO sent forth a champion to represent them in F3 Aggieland's Fitness Benchmark. Herculeans competed against each other in their own category earning points for their AO based on their composite score.

Scoring
Points were awarded based on ranking as follows:
1st place - 5 points
2nd place - 4 points
3rd place - 3 points
4th place - 2 points
5th place - 1 point

Q-Source - Mutual Competence (Q3.2)
QOD: How might you improve your competence or others to make things more "mutual"? The General Alignment Of Skill Within A Shared Leadership Team
Competence is critical to Group Prosperity Inculcating Mutual Competence within a SLT begins with the Q. He cannot set and maintain high Standards for his Team unless he can meet them himself. This is a basic premise of Leadership by example that is reflected in the F3 admonition don’t Q it if you can’t do it. A Leader must be individually Competent to call his followers forth to Mutual Competence.
On paper, this sounds both obvious and necessary, but in practice it is one of the most difficult challenges a Leader faces. As a man rises through the Leadership ranks of a Group, he will find an ever increasing amounts of his time being taken by things that have little to do with Group’s Missional-Essential Tasks. As his responsibilities grow, his opportunities to stay Competent shrink. To ensure that he is able to Skillfully perform his METs, he needs to build Routines that enable him to continually Practice the Skills that made him a Leader in the first place.

The Leadership Skills are the four capabilities of Effective Leadership that enable a man do what a Leader does. They are:

Vision: The ability to recognize Advantage and determine the Movement required to achieve it.

Articulation: The clear and compelling communication of a Vision to others so they understand where they are going and why.

Persuasion: The initiation of first Movement by convincing people to overcome their natural attachment to the Status Quo.

Exhortation: The energizing encouragement that enables people to overcome Obstacles and sustain Momentum toward Advantage.
——
The Leadership Virtues are the five Habits and Ethics of moral excellence that enable a man to be who a Leader is. They are:

Candor: The Habit of graciously telling and demanding the hard truth to ensure voluntary and honest Movement.

Commitment: Unwavering loyalty to the Group and determination to accomplish its Mission over the long term.

Consistency: The steadfastness of character, standards, and actions over time that builds trust and reliability.

Contentment: The emotional stability that comes from the pursuit of lasting Joy rather than fleeting Personal Comfort.

Courage: The Habit of overcoming fear through Preparedness and self-control to transform hardship into grace.
——
To Lead Right a person must be both an Effective and Virtuous Leader. Not one or the other: both.

In the Q2.3 we learned that Missionality is Essential to Living Right because a man’s IMPACT is greatest when he is Serving in the High Impact Zone of his D2X–the intersection of his Dolphin (the Task he was born to do best) and his Daffodil (the people-group he was born to best Serve). This is where his forcible contact will be the most Effective. Through experience, the HIM learns that the farther he strays from his D2X, the less IMPACT he has.
To Target is to give the greatest gift a man can provide, the freedom to move beyond himself into his High Impact Zone for it is only that he will find true Joy.


Targeting moves a man beyond himself 
The Joy of Serving by seeking Advantage for others bolsters a HIM’s commitment to consistently and deliberately place himself behind his Creator and Community–what F3 calls Living Third. Similar to how carrying the message of AA to other alcoholics enables someone to continue practicing its principles in his own life, Targeting moves a man beyond himself to what Maslow described as the very highest level of human consciousness, or to what what Christ called the greater love, the laying down of one’s life for his friends.
To Target is to give the greatest gift a man can provide, the freedom to move beyond himself into his High Impact Zone for it is only that he will find true Joy.



A Targeted man moves in relational rhythm
We usually think of rhythm in relation to musical beat and tempo. Rhythm is critical to music. A guitarist may accurately play each individual note in a song, but without rhythm it won’t sound right. If far enough out of rhythm, it might not even sound like music at all but rather a discordant jumbling of disconnected sounds.
The individual components of our own lives must be working in in sync for them to function properly. If our Queen is out of control, our M decelerates. When we don’t Meet, our Shorties suffer. If our Jester rules over us, our Mammon is in disarray.
A man’s life is a single thing comprised of many components that must be rhythmically integrated.
