THANG 2
🎾 Gauntlet Relay (Tennis Court)
Objective: 5-part group relay challenge focused on movement, coordination, and teamwork.
1️⃣ Run & Touch Fence
• Everyone in the group runs to the opposite fence of the court
• Touch it, then return back together
2️⃣ 20 Side-Straddle Hops
• Each group member completes 20 SSH (in place)
• Once everyone finishes, run together to the opposite fence and back
3️⃣ 30-Second “World’s Together” Hold
• As a group, hold a 30-second wall sit or low squat
• Count together as one unit: “1… 2… 3…” up to 30
• After completing, run together to the opposite fence and back
4️⃣ Rest Round
• Group decides how long to rest — as long or short as you want
• When ready, run together to the opposite fence and return
5️⃣ Bucket Ball Finale
• Several balls are scattered across the opposite side of the court
• One teammate at a time sprints, grabs a ball, and places it in the team bucket
• While waiting your turn: perform air squats
• After your sprint: plank for the six until the whole group is done
• Continue until every member has retrieved a ball and placed it in the bucket

Summary of Accountability Q-Source

	1.	Blind Spots require help. Unlike moral weaknesses, Blind Spots can’t be fixed alone. The HIM recognizes his need for others to help cover what he can’t see.
	2.	Accountability is external. It requires submission to objective Standards, and enforcement from someone else. Self-accountability is a myth.
	3.	Standards must be binary and inarguable. If there’s wiggle room, it’s not a Standard—it’s an aspiration. Clear Standards create clarity of action.
	4.	Enforcement and Consequence are painful but necessary. Shame, though unpleasant, often provides the wake-up call that leads to long-term change and growth.
	5.	The Shield Lock is essential. No HIM fights his Blind Spots alone. An Effective Shield Lock of like-minded men offers mutual Accountability, trust, and shared movement forward.

Lasts 10 minutes. All coupons lined up at half court. Number off PAX 1 and PAX 2. All PAX 1 on one baseline, all PAX 2 on opposite baseline. When Q yells start, all PAX begin a circuit of 10 Merkins, 10 Shoulder Taps (2 is 1), 10 Mississippi high plank, and 5 burpees. When a PAX completes the circuit, he races to center court, grabs a coupon, deposits it inside the opposite team’s 3-point line, as far as humanly possible beyond the opposite team’s baseline, then runs back to complete another circuit. All PAX continue in same fashion, doing their circuit, taking coupons from inside their team’s 3-point line far and wide around Brazos County, and depositing it inside the other team’s 3-point line in orbit around the black hole at the center of the galaxy. BOHICA until time is called. Team with fewest coupons inside their 3-point line wins.

“Strong teams don’t happen by accident—they’re built on high standards and collective accountability.”

Just like a man needs personal accountability to grow, a team needs shared standards to thrive. Without them, teams drift—they lose direction, momentum, and purpose. That’s why the leader, the Q, must do more than just set the standard—he must enforce it and exceed it.

If you, as the Q, drop below the standard, you’ve just told the team that the standard doesn’t matter. Leadership by example isn’t optional—it’s the foundation of trust.

Now, enforcing standards means consequences. And on a team, there are only two that matter: probation, and if that fails—termination. It sounds harsh, but it’s necessary. A man who won’t row—or worse, rows in the wrong direction—slows the whole team down.

We call those men Kimonos and Toxics. The Kimono values comfort over mission—he’s dead weight. The Toxic? He’s a strong force, just pulling against the team’s purpose. Both will decelerate your group and must be dealt with.

But here’s the difference: you never give up on the man who wants to grow. If he’s willing to work, you train him, guide him, invest in him. The Q always has hope for the willing.

In the end, leadership is about love. Love that challenges, holds the line, and helps each man become who he was meant to be—even if that means letting go when necessary. That’s how strong teams are built.

Questions to ponder:

Socratic

18 PAX, Including YHC, decided that the best place to be on the day before Father's Day, was showing their families that they are Strong, fit, and capable providers. There were bout 6 PAX that planned on attending but couldn't and each one expressed the pain of their FOMO. However, the greater Katy, Richmond, and Ft. Bend Counties were well represented by men that wanted to compete and show their families that they still possessed the qualities that made their M's fall in love with them and embodied the spirit that they hoped to pass on to their 2.0s.

All that is great, but the F3's Strongest PAX was really about one thing: raising money to research treatments and cures for children born with congenital heart defects. We all tell our families and friends that we don't care if we have a boy or a girl, as long as they are healthy. 80,000 parents every year, are forced to endure the news that their precious newborn has something wrong. If you have ever experienced this pain, our hearts go out to you and your loved ones. I cannot imagine the fear that would rush through me, if I heard that my child may not survive. It is for those parents, and those precious babies, that we gathered together. We want to be a part of the solution. To be a small light in the darkness, and hope that our small contribution will change the life of at least one family for the better.

I know the McDaniels family would trade everything for one more day with Graeme. So, today we honored that precious boy and so many just like him, by lifting heavy stuff, competing, and donating just over $3700 to the Grame McDaniel Foundation. https://graememcdanielfoundation.org/ 
On top of that, we were able to put $500 in the F3 MKT coffers. Having the ability to do what we did and further the mission of F3, is a priceless feeling as well.

Huge Thank you to the Raising Cane's Team that came out and provided Water, Lemonade, toys, and helped with the timekeeping and judging. That company is so much more than just great chicken. They are a community stalwart and a champion of so many different noble causes. I hope they had as much fun as the rest of us did.

Another HUGE thank you to the Katy City Council, Katy Parks Dept, and the Parks Committee. They not only allowed us the use of the park, but waived the $160 in fees that we would have spent on rental fees. Instead that money gets passed on to the kids that need it.

Thank you to all of our volunteers that showed up early to help set this up, run the timers, keep track of reps, and encourage us during the pain of this competition. The epic video will also soon be provided by our very own Kingpin. Zelda donated those epic freaking patches too. The gratitude that we all have for the people that made this happen is immense. Thank you!

Positive Habit Transfer (PHT)
* 3 kinds of habits: negative/bad, positive, and neutral. A negative or bad habit damages the individual and in many cases negatively affects the people close to them.  Example: texting while driving. Neutral habits are neither damaging nor advantageous, with significant effects and at worst a waste of time. Example: chewing gum while driving. Positive habits (Bricks) are regular tendencies that are advantageous to the individual and their Concentrica. Example: wearing a seat belt while driving 
* Bad Habits are easy to slip into, but hard to break. Positive Habits are hard to develop, but easy to slip out of. Most people need forcible contact from another person in order to replace their negative Habits with positive ones. This help is best delivered in the form of the Positive Habit Transfer (PHT).

Missionality: Dolphin, Daffodil, and the HIZ

Men, we just pushed ourselves physically—but F3 is about more than fitness. It’s about purpose. Let me hit you with three words that can change your impact: Dolphin, Daffodil, and HIZ.

⸻

1. The Dolphin – What You Do Best
Your Dolphin is your strongest natural skill. It’s the thing you do better than almost anyone else—often without even thinking about it.
Maybe it’s leading. Maybe it’s teaching, organizing, fixing, encouraging, solving.
But whatever it is comes as naturally to you as swimming does to a dolphin.

If you’re unsure what your Dolphin is, ask your brothers. It’s may be that they see it.

⸻

2. The Daffodil – Where Your Heart Is
Your Daffodil is the part of the world you’re passionate about.
It could be fatherhood, mentoring young men, building stronger marriages, fighting addiction, helping the homeless—whatever group or cause stirs your heart.

It’s where you feel called to serve—not out of duty, but desire.

⸻

3. The High Impact Zone (HIZ) – Where You’re Meant to Be
Your High Impact Zone, or HIZ, is where your Dolphin and your Daffodil overlap. Also called the D2X.
It’s the sweet spot where your gifts meet the world’s needs.
When you’re in your HIZ, you’re not just going through the motions—you’re leading a life that changes lives.

That’s where you become the man you were made to be.

⸻

Because many of us often don’t take clear time to sit down and think clearly about your Dolphin, Daffodil, and HIZ, I want us to break into groups and do two things now, and one thing later. 

First identify your dolphin, daffodil, and HIZ to the men in your group. If you don’t know what those things are for you, say so.

Second, each of you should say something to one other PAX that will encourage them as they pursue their mission through their own Dolphin and Daffodil. Let it be awkward, but just say something encouraging.

Third (the thing later), commit to reaching out to a PAX in your small group before the next 30/30 to see how they’re living into their mission.

Q Source:
Frostbite told us about dolphins, daphodils, staying in the HIZ and out of the goo. 

The HIM has a good grasp on both his Dolphin and his Daffodil, and spends most of his time working at the point where they intersect, which we call the D2X . The D2X is the sweet spot that is at the dead center of a man’s High Impact Zone. It is where he will have the most IMPACT if he acts with Deliberatude and lives in dangerous disregard of the risk of Failure and embarrassment.
The HIM uses Preparedness to resist straying from his Mission
The powerful results a HIM produces working within his HIZ creates a challenge to his Missionality. His IMPACT within the Groups he Serves will soon result in requests that he undertake Tasks that range far outside of his D2X. No matter how compelling the underlying need sounds, the HIM should quickly and firmly decline to do so.

Here are the four reasons why:

1) He will disappoint the asker

When an excited well-meaning person compliments the HIM on how fantastic his efforts are within his D2X, he should be ready for the next sentence, which will sound something like this: “so, I got to thinking how perfect you would be for this critical, challenging life-changing opportunity to do the same thing (although differently) for this other (wholly unrelated) group of people.”

The asker reasons that the HIM’s success within his D2X arises primarily from him being a successful person, rather than being the result of his disciplined Missionality. Ergo, to the asker, the HIM will succeed at everything else regardless of its relation to what he does well. There is a certain logic to that, but the HIM knows the truth. He knows he can’t possibly perform outside of his D2X the way he does within it and that the asker will inevitably be disappointed. Sure, the asker will also be disappointed when the HIM declines the offer, but not nearly as much as he will be when he ends up mailing it in on the new thing, the asker’s thing.

And that’s what we end up doing when we take things on outside of our D2X, we mail it in.

2) He will deny service to his own Daffodil

When a HIM succumbs to the temptation of the well-meaning asker and takes on something outside of his D2X, there will be a consequence to his own Daffodil. Every minute he spends mailing it in outside of his D2X is lost to the time he has available for his own Daffodil. It’s hard to calculate the opportunity cost on that. Particularly when you consider how much longer it takes to mail in mediocre performance than it does to dynamically provide a great performance.

3) He will box out the right HIM

4) Ultimately, it will be a Joyless experience

Unless you are the kind of man who does the hard things first every day, you probably do what you love to do first and leave what you hate until later in the day (at which point you ultimately blow it off or try to get somebody else to do it). But eventually you end up having to do those hated things, and it is always Joyless drudgery.

But, because he’s a Pro, he also stays ready for the unexpected–and that is the pressure from within that is generated by his own pride and ego trying to convince him that even though this is not a job for him, he is the only man who can do this job–even if it kills him.

The graveyards are full of indispensable men and yet the Earth keeps turning. Just say no. Stay Missional.

Q-source: 
This week’s Q-source is about Missionality. The focus is on finding one’s giftings and one’s passions, the things one is naturally gifted at and the people and/or causes that one is naturally inclined towards serving. The Q-source also made me think of some advice I’ve heard elsewhere, which was “excel at the revealed things,” and that seems to be the core attitude of what is meant in discussing the “comfort zone.” Lean into the things that have been revealed in you, the giftings, the passions, perhaps even the talents that you may have for situations that might actually make you uncomfortable (for example, being affirmed as a good public speaker even if you don’t actually like public speaking). I struggle to lean into this in my schedule. Ideally, I would form my time around the things I excel at. Instead, I often allocate more time for the things I’m not as good at because I know that I can do “good enough” with less time where I’m skilled, but that reduces my effectiveness. The Q-source also made me think about Nehemiah from the Bible. Nehemiah understood his giftings (his ability to organize people and resources, along with the position to be able to organize them) and his passion (helping restore the city of Jerusalem). He understood the call to excel at the revealed things and be diligent with the task at hand. But he also understood not to be distracted with other tasks or by naysayers. Missionality


The culture paints the Comfort Zone as a lazy refuge, urging people to “get out” to reach their full potential, but F3 challenges this notion with a deeper truth. Rather than abandon the Comfort Zone, a man should lean into his High Impact Zone (HIZ)—the place where his natural wiring, or Dolphin, intersects with his heart for a particular group, or Daffodil. The daffodil symbolizes renewal, hope, and new beginnings, often representing the arrival of spring and the promise of positive change. This intersection, known as his D2X, is where his Skills are most refined and his IMPACT most powerful. To leave this zone in pursuit of constant novelty, as Goo Nation urges, is to trade effectiveness for the illusion of growth.
Culture mistakenly equates Joy with Happiness and tells men their dissatisfaction comes from not chasing new things—when in truth, it stems from not living with Purpose. The HIM resists this pull by embracing Missionality, staying anchored to the Tasks that align with his HIZ. These Tasks are not arbitrary; they’re the deliberate outgrowth of how a man is hard-wired to Serve.
When others notice a HIM’s effectiveness, they often ask him to take on things outside his Mission, wrongly assuming he’s universally excellent. But working outside his HIZ only leads to mediocre results, the neglect of his true calling, and robbing another man of his own D2X opportunity. Worse, it becomes a Joyless burden, squeezed into the edges of his schedule and devoid of the energy and passion his true Mission stirs.
To stay Missional, a HIM must say “no” with conviction, even when flattery, guilt, or ego tempt him to say yes. He must discern between true needs (like a Diaper Changer) and distractions that dilute his effectiveness. He trains himself to anticipate both external temptation and internal pride, knowing that the desire to feel irreplaceable is a seductive lie. His Shield Lock keeps him grounded with the necessary words: “get over yourself.”
The HIM’s strength lies in focused discipline, not scattered busyness. He understands that his greatest impact comes not from doing many things, but doing the right things with excellence and consistency. Living Right means doubling down on one’s Purpose, not chasing cultural myths of “expansion.” In doing so, he finds not only maximum effectiveness—but deep, resilient Joy.

Q Source Q2.3 - MISSIONALITY

The cultural narrative often views the comfort zone—where a person functions with ease and familiarity—as a limiting, fear-based place one must escape to grow. Influential voices like Oprah champion the idea that true self-actualization comes from risking discomfort and trying new things. This belief system, labeled as “Goo Nation,” prioritizes transient happiness over deep, lasting joy, and pressures people to abandon their natural strengths in pursuit of constant novelty.
F3 offers a counterpoint: instead of fleeing the comfort zone, individuals should identify and work deeply within their High Impact Zone (HIZ)—where their natural abilities have the greatest effect. This isn’t about stagnation, but about consistent Practice to grow one’s Skill in areas where they are hardwired to excel.
A man’s purpose-driven work, or Task, is formed by the intersection of two hard-wired truths:
* His Dolphin: his unique gift—the thing he does better than anything else, and better than most people. A dolphin’s Dolphin is being able to swim. This gift is innate and best refined through Practice. 
* His Daffodil: the specific group of people he is born to Serve. While the HIM (High Impact Man) cares for all people, he has a unique love and calling toward his Daffodil.
Where these two meet is called the D2X—the sweet spot at the very center of his HIZ. This is where a man has the greatest IMPACT and where he should spend most of his energy. Straying outside of the D2X, even with good intentions, diminishes effectiveness, drains joy, and potentially blocks someone else better suited from stepping in.
Saying "no" to opportunities outside one’s D2X is a disciplined act of Missionality. The HIM resists external flattery and internal ego, staying focused on his unique calling. Preparedness helps him stay grounded, joyful, and effective, rather than reactive and scattered like the Amateur who constantly chases happiness by leaving his comfort zone.
In short: Rather than trying to be everything to everyone, a man finds the most purpose and joy by identifying his Dolphin, Serving his Daffodil, and operating within his D2X—where he was meant to make his highest impact.
Do you know what your Dolphin and Daffodil are? If so, how are you seeking to use them? If not, who can you ask in your life to help you name them?

Q-source:
The Q source this week is about impact, about using your proximity to someone to serve them and help them move towards improved circumstances. I wanted to take things in a slightly different, but related, direction. I’ve had discussions with friends recently about leadership and authority, and a friend pointed out that authority, accountability, and responsibility are a package deal. Authority can be taken (though this might impossible for one to force their authority on another while acting alone), it can be conferred by a higher authority, or it can be earned/given by the people to be led. But, to have authority and lead people, you also need to have the means of improving their circumstances (and you also need to prove to them that you have the means). Even if someone agrees that what you are seeking is an improvement upon their current circumstances, they have no reason to follow if you cannot show them that you have the means to get them there (and this is related to the Get Right that we’ve talked about previously). But, if you convince them and they accept your authority, they are also giving you responsibility over them in some way and they will hold you accountable if you mislead them or can’t get them to the goal. So, reach out and serve, but remember to count the cost of leading others and stay humble and wise so you will lead them well.

As Pax participate in the Thang, they should think about that person when they get ready to put Cindies down and instead dig a little deeper and give a little more and go a little further. Each pax will farmers carry walk cindies around the big loop circling the park (.33 miles each lap). Every tenth of a mile was marked by chalk. The F3 Nation article on "IMPACT (Q2.1)" defines impactful leadership as deliberate, forcible engagement to create transformative change. A High Impact Man (HIM) must be proximate to those he influences, particularly "Survivors" (men oppressed by circumstances) and "Sad Clowns" (men stuck in stagnation), initiating action to spark change. Only "Servants," who prioritize others’ advantage, can lead this movement, living "third" by placing Creator and community above self, fostering joy and invigorating male community leadership.

3 takeaways:
Proximity is Key: Effective leadership requires close physical or relational contact to create impactful change in others.
Deliberate Action: A High Impact Man must initiate forcible engagement to help "Survivors" (oppressed men) and "Sad Clowns" (stagnant men) overcome their challenges.
Servant Leadership: True impact comes from prioritizing others’ needs over self, living "third" to foster community and spiritual growth.

Opening Energy / Acknowledgment

Every so often in a man’s life, he discovers something that gives him excitement and momentum.
It’s as if he’s discovered fire all over again.


Joining F3 has been exactly that for me.
It’s the most excited I’ve been in a while.


Since joining, I’ve been moved by each and every one of you and drawn toward the creative lessons from the Q Source.

What makes the Q Source so special to me is that I’ve been practicing many of its principles for years — in some form or fashion — without even realizing it had a name.
I think God may have led me here. I feel at home.


So I wanted to lead a weight loss challenge that involves all the things I’ve practiced and that has changed my life in so many ways.

It incorporates principles like the King, the Queen, the Daily Red Pill, Preparedness, Consistency, Positive Habit Transfer… and the most important, the Jester.


This was an 8-week challenge with 36 PAX.
We did weigh-ins, weekly check-ins, before/after photos.

I want to let everyone know

Everyone worked hard.
Most of you lost weight, built discipline, and gained tools you’ll carry forward.


The ultimate goal of this challenge is a lifestyle change, not just a challenge or a diet. It is new mindset shift to integrate these things into your new life and age with finesse. It’s something serious, real and has to be practiced far beyond 8 weeks.

You’ve all won something here.

Q SOURCE

What are some opportunities you see to serve others around you; do you think you are prepared to do so?


Living Right is the second quadrant of the QSource and represents a HIM’s dedication to Purposefulness—a life committed to bringing external Advantage through deliberate self-sacrifice. Whereas Getting Right aligns a man internally through Fitness, Fellowship, and Faith, Living Right is about his outward IMPACT on others. Purpose demands more than intention; it demands movement, service, and a willingness to place Creator and Community above self. A man who is still fighting to survive cannot serve others—his energy is consumed by staying afloat.

But when a man takes the Red Pill and begins to Get Right, he eventually has the capacity to Live Third—behind his SkyQ and his fellow man. This transition moves him from being a Survivor to a Servant, the two poles on the Sur-Ser Continuum. Most men, however, live somewhere in the middle, posing as functional while quietly desperate, capsized beneath the surface. These are the Sad Clowns—externally stable, internally sinking.

The HIM is the force of disruption that reaches into this mediocrity and pulls men toward hope. His own alignment and strength allow him to carry others, and in doing so, he himself remains Right. Paradoxically, his abandonment of self-preservation strengthens his personal integrity. Living Right isn’t just noble—it’s necessary, because it’s the only way a man becomes what he was truly created to be.

There are 9 landings on the tower. Each round, the PAX start with a prescribed exercise, and for each landing, they do an exercise with ascending reps until the top-- from 1 rep at the bottom to 9 reps at the top. After a 10 count breather at the top, PAX descend the tower with descending reps, from 8 to 1. 

* ROUND 1: Copperhead Squats going up, Jump Squats going down

* ROUND 2: Merkins going up, Mountain Climbers coming down 

* Q SOURCE: 
    * MEETING, the public manifestation of Faith
    * Every musician plays to his audience whether he realizes it or not. What effect on the heart of a Shepherd to look into the front row of his flock and see the strongest men he knows in his Group sitting there attentively? Would that not make him bold, to know that he has the support of the men upon whom he would most be able to rely in the confrontation of Hardship? Would that not make him more likely to be Candid and graciously tell the hard Truth?
    * Conversely, the absence of HIMs in the pews leads the Shepherd to grow timid in his willingness to speak boldly and provide Truth to his flock. What costs come with social interaction and do the pros outweigh the cons?


A HIM (High Impact Man) does not seek truth alone—he expresses his faith publicly through Meeting, despite the logistical frustrations and emotional resistance it often brings. Though sitting through services may feel uncomfortable or unproductive, he persists because he knows Meeting isn’t about personal happiness, but about fulfilling his role as a leader. In spiritual valleys, when a man feels least like participating, Meeting becomes most vital. It allows him to draw strength from others and, more importantly, to forget himself in service to a Brother in greater need. That selfless moment often lifts him back to his own spiritual mountaintop.

Meeting, like Prayer and Study, is a habitual practice that increases a man's skill in living out his Faith. A Virtuous Leader leads not just with skills but with moral excellence rooted in a belief system, and competence in that system requires consistent practice. Through Meeting, a man strengthens his legacy, one that can influence others long after he’s gone.

Additionally, the HIM’s presence holds the spiritual Shepherd accountable to speak the Truth boldly and with Candor. Without strong men in the pews, a Shepherd may dilute the hard truths to avoid conflict. Deeper Dive: “Spiritual but Not Religious” — A Real Belief System

1. A Belief System can be Spiritual
•	A belief system is simply the conviction that there’s a force—supernatural or natural—that imposes order, meaning, and consequences on human life.
•	Even if someone denies organized religion, they still live by guiding principles about right, wrong, purpose, and consequence. That’s a belief system.

Example from the passage: Bob Dylan doesn’t claim a religion, but he finds spiritual guidance in music. His songs explore the same core questions religions address: “What happens when we die?” and “How should we live?” That makes his worldview a belief system—even if it’s nontraditional.

⸻

2. “Spiritual” People Still Wrestle with the Big Questions
	•	Everyone—religious or not—has to face the “What-What”:
•	What happens when I die?
•	What does that mean for how I should live?

“Spiritual but not religious” individuals often seek answers to these in nature, music, philosophy, relationships, or even personal intuition.
	•	These answers shape how they lead, how they use power, and how they view accountability.

3. Leadership Without Structure Becomes Dangerous
	•	The problem isn’t whether your belief system is spiritual or religious. It’s whether it has depth, guardrails, and consistency.
	•	Leaders who rely solely on instinct or emotion risk drifting into self-serving behavior.
	•	True faith—spiritual or religious—must be practiced and studied to have real impact.

What does a man need to set his direction, find purpose, and lead?


A man cannot Get Right without Faith—a right relationship with his Creator—and no amount of worldly leadership skill can compensate for the absence of a deeper moral framework. While belief systems vary, every man must wrestle with the same two questions: What happens when I die? and What does that mean about how I should live? These are the "What-What," and a man’s answers to them form the foundation of his Belief System, whether religious, philosophical, or instinctual. Without this foundation, power corrupts easily, and even the most Effective Leader becomes a danger to his Group, as unrestrained authority inevitably serves self, not others.

Virtue, the restraint that channels leadership for good, cannot be self-generated; it arises from a man’s submission to something higher than himself. To grow in Faith, the HIM must Study—not just accept—his Belief System, testing its principles with the same rigor he applies to his profession. Just as a lawyer or doctor continually deepens their knowledge and sharpens their skill, so too must a man Practice his Faith or risk its Deceleration. Study is not about blind devotion but about honest scrutiny, learning from those who have asked and answered the What-What before.

Faith, like law or medicine, is a dynamic discipline: learning leads to doing, doing reveals gaps in understanding, and those gaps send a man back to Study. Without this cycle, Faith becomes stagnant and brittle—incapable of supporting the weight of real life. For the HIM, Faith is not a vague spirituality or a set of comforting beliefs, but a lived, practiced alignment with eternal truth. It is the difference between being a man who seems right and one who is right—and between leaving a legacy of power or one of purpose.

Thang 2: Q-Source: Study
How do you make the decisions you make, every day? I don’t mean the easy decisions like, “Am I going to wear the blue shirt or the grey shirt?” I mean the decisions that matter, like, “Am I going to flip this guy off in traffic and tailgate him or drive like a sane human being?” “Am I going to lose my temper with my wife and kids, or am I going to listen, comfort them, and have compassion on them?” “Am I going to eat this entire box of cookies, or stick with my eating plan?”

All of those decisions should be made based on your morals and your values. But for morals and values to have real meaning, they have to be absolute. My cholesterol numbers are an absolute truth. A year ago, it was dangerously high. With regular exercise and cutting sugar, it decreased by almost 25% in 9 months. That’s an absolute truth. If I stop exercising and start drinking soda every day, it’s going to go right back up. I can deny that it would be “that bad” for me, but again, the statistics don’t lie.

Similarly, the values and morals that inform our everyday decisions need to be absolute. I either cursed at the guy who cut me off on the highway, or I forgave him and said, “I wish he were more careful but maybe he has a good reason to be driving like that.” I either told my boss a lie about the progress of my current project at work, or I was candid about the problems we’re facing so that he stays informed and can help me if things take a turn for the worse.

I posted this a few days ago and I’ll repost it for emphasis: Self-esteem is the reputation you have with yourself. If the actions you take when no one else is watching don’t match up with the things you know inside you’re supposed to be doing, your self-esteem will suffer the consequences. You won’t believe in yourself. What you do in the dark never truly hides, because your character, confidence, and values will always only reflect the things that you know to be true.

So where do we get our values? When we’re children, we get them from our parents, our family, or a similar source. We learn our values from someone bigger than we are. That needs to still be true when we’re men - we still need to get our values from someone bigger than we are. For many of us that’s God, for others, it’s Allah, for still others, it might be Buddha. Most of us start learning about those things from someone else, but if I stop there, then I’m relying entirely on someone else’s knowledge of my Creator. I’m fallible enough that I don’t need someone else just taking my word for it, so what comes next?

All of those “bigger things” have writings - the Bible, the Qur’an, the Tripitaka. Those writings are where we derive our values. As a Christian, my values are to strive to be more like Jesus Christ by following his teachings. It’s not enough for me to listen to a preacher, or a pastor, or an elder. Those are just men, like me. They make mistakes, they get things wrong, and I can’t depend on them for absolute values. I have to read, I have to study, and I have to make those values my own.

Faith, the third component of the Get Right:

Faith is a man’s right relationship with his Creator, and without it, no man can truly Get Right—let alone Live, Lead, or Leave Right. Alongside Fitness and Fellowship, Faith completes the triad that forms the foundation of proper personal alignment. While Fellowship connects him with others, Faith anchors a man to something beyond himself, reminding him he is not the king of his own world. Without Faith, a man rules from a fragile throne of pride and control, eventually brought low by life’s inevitable storms.

Through Prayer, Study, and Meeting, the HIM pursues answers to life’s deepest questions—the What-What: What happens when I die? and What does that mean about how I should live? This search is ancient, human, and necessary, not just to make sense of the world but to prepare for both the expected and the unknown. Prayer, in particular, is the HIM’s weapon against anxiety, transforming fear and worry into Hope rooted in something greater than himself. When the storms of life rise unexpectedly, the man who is anchored in Faith will not be capsized. He does not simply survive—he Accelerates, because he knows he is not alone, and he is not in control. And that realization, paradoxically, is what gives him the greatest strength.

What truth does the HIM need. The What-What is the amalgam of the two questions a Pro has asked from the beginning of time. The first WHAT is what will happen when I die? The second WHAT is what does that mean about the way I should live? To be in Right relationship with his Creator, the HIM continually seeks the answers to the what what

Despite all that modern man has learned of the material world, the Pro’s quest for knowledge of what lies beyond it still persists. Though we seem to have unlocked so many of the secrets of what can be known of the world we can see around us, man alone cannot answer the What-What for himself. He can only do that through Prayer, by talking with his Creator in order to build his Faith.

It's important to note that the "Bring Sally Up" push-up workout should be challenging, but also manageable. If you're new to push-ups, it may be helpful to start with a modified version or to work on building up your strength and endurance before attempting the full workout.

THE MAMMON

A man is designed to work, not only to provide for himself and his family but to serve and strengthen his Community through his unique contributions. Work, or Mammon, is a sustaining relationship that aligns a man with purpose—but it is also dangerous if misprioritized. Mammon is deceptively easy, affirming, and replaceable, which tempts a man to elevate it above more vital relationships like his marriage, his children, and his brothers-in-arms. However, the HIM (High Impact Man) recognizes this trap and keeps work in its proper place: important, but not primary.
Mammon must be treated with Deliberatude—approached not just as a function, but as a connection to manage with discipline and awareness. When a man allows work to replace his roles as husband, father, or brother, he commits relational malpractice and jeopardizes the very people for whom he labors. Workaholism is the Jester’s snare—seductive because of its structure, feedback, and control—but ultimately empty if it replaces real relational depth. The HIM prepares for this battle and refuses to let the ease of Mammon distract from his true purpose. He works to live, not the other way around—always placing those he loves and serves before the job that sustains them.

WHY WE DO THE MURPH CHALLENGE
IN HONOR OF LT MICHAEL P. MURPHY

The Murph Challenge is not just a physical test, but also a mental and emotional one.
Participants are pushed to their limits and are encouraged to keep pushing through the pain and exhaustion, just as Lieutenant Murphy did during his final moments. The event is held annually on Memorial Day, and people from all over the world come together to honor Lieutenant Murphy and all those who have given their lives in service to our country. The Murph Challenge is a powerful reminder of the sacrifices made by our military and a testament to the strength and resilience of the human spirit. Never Forget.

The Murph workout goes as follows:
*   1-mile run
*   100 pull-ups
*   200 push-ups
*   300 air squats (bodyweight squats)
*   1-mile run The entire workout is designed to be done wearing a 20lb weighted vest, to stimulate the body armor Murphey would have worn.

Modifications:  1. Ditch the vest   
2.  Break up your reps (I.e. 10 pull ups, 20 push ups, 30 squats x 10 rounds)

Whetstone- the Vertical relationship between Men-

Sharpening Other Men: The Power of Vertical Relationships

A man is like a knife—both are made to cut, but neither is effective unless they are sharpened. In life, sharpening happens through intentional relationships between men—where an older, more seasoned man (the Stone) sharpens a younger man (the Blade).

Why It Matters:
	•	An unsharpened man is dull—ineffective as a leader and unprepared for life’s challenges.
•	A man’s desire to grow and lead well must be whetted—his appetite stirred—by another man who challenges and invests in him.

What Sharpening Requires (The 3 P’s):
1.	Proximity – They must meet in person. Eye contact, tough conversations, and real presence matter.
2.	Purpose – It’s not just hanging out. The goal is growth: building discipline, preparing for life, and owning responsibility.
3.	Periodicity – It has to happen regularly, but not so often it loses its edge. Pain and discomfort are part of the process, so deliberate commitment is key.

The Benefit for Both Men:•	
The Blade gains a sharper edge—ready to lead and make an impact.
•	The Stone grows too—as he teaches, he becomes more aligned, less hypocritical, and stronger in his own habits and guardrails.
Helping another man grow actually sharpens you. It’s not a one-way street. This principle reflects truth found even in recovery communities: when we teach and live it out, we become it ourselves.

Final Takeaway:

If you’re a man who wants to lead, don’t walk alone. Be a Stone. Find a Blade. And be sharpened in the process. Deliberate male mentorship is essential to becoming who you were made to be.

Q plays "Thunderstruck" by ACDC. PAX complete 1 standard Merkin for every "thunder!" that is heard in the song. Plank during the rest of the song. Awesome way to end a workout and just make sure any juice that's left is burned away.

Thang 2— Lindsays aka 40’s— Dips/Curls for the Girls
Lindsays are a high-rep variation of Elevens. You start with 30 reps of one exercise and 10 reps of another exercise OYO, then subtract 5 reps from the first exercise and add five reps from the second. Repeat OYO until you have 10 reps of the first exercise and 30 reps of the second. The sum must always add up to 40. Example: Lindsays with Dips and Curls for the girls starts you with 30 Dips and 10 Curls, then 25 Dips and 15 Curls, then 20 Dips and 20 Curls, then 15 Dips and 25 Curls, then 10 Dips and 30 Curls.

Tennis court mash up.
2 teams, racing against each other, have to fill 1 bucket each up with baseballs. We had two teams of 10 which we switched/reprgaanized for the 2nd round.

Beginning:
Each team member, one at a time has to sprint across the court to go grab a baseball on the other side, run back, put it in the bucket and the team al together has to do the corresponding work out in the big board before sending another person to go run to grab a ball, come back and do the next corresponding work out.  So…( 1 baseball everyone in the group does the 1 workout, 2 balls, # 2 workout together, 3 and 3 so on and so forth until you complete all of them together.

This workout tests communication skills, cardio, team work and just hard work and high effort.

Once all the balls are in the bucket each team then has to unload the bucket one at a time by running them to the other side, setting them on 10 seperate cones before coming back to tag the next player in order for them to deliver the next ball.  To finish, All players must be sitting down in order to complete the assigned workout once all balls are placed on the cones.

This workout had everyone breathing hard and included a lot of cardio. This was a good workout for all included even those who were I hured and modified! The kids crushed it and we had a blast getting betters.

The consequence for the losing team is 10 burpees and 20 burpees for the 2nd round losing team. The winning team does tree huggers until all burpees are complete.

 - Of course! We strive to work and prepare together and catch one another's blindspots and shortcomings. Men coming together to form teams progresses everything in the community. 

3. Can a man begin the fight against adversity before he encounters it?

There are 8 different stations (marked by cones, lights, and signs). Depending on identity assignment PAX worked their way through the stations in order as follows (Rifle Carry Coupon between stations - modify to farmer carry or shoulder carry):

After completing 4 stations, PAX got to fight Bowser.

What does fighting Bowser entail, you ask?

- First, Pax rolls a 🎲 
Whatever number was rolled becomes the Hit Points that Pax will inflict upon Bowser.
- Next, Pax attempted to hit Bowser’s weak spot (frisbee tied to fence) with a “fireball” (Softball). If Pax hits the target, they were supposed to record their score on the whiteboard (epic Q fail choosing to use dry erase board instead of chalk because markers stopped working due to dampness in morning air 😡), and then continue to do stations initially assigned to other brother (Marios did Luigi’s and vice versa)
- if Pax missed the target, they had to do burpees equal to number of dice roll in order to inflict the HP, then they continued to do other stations.

Bowser HP Calculation: # of Pax * 3.5 (Median dice roll outcomes) * 4 (expected Pax to finish 4 laps - 2 of each Mario/Luigi).

So Bowser HP was 196.

Intent was to add all PAX HP scores as we went and when total reached 196, Bowser was defeated. Pax were supposed to AMRAP the loops until Bowser’s downfall. Instead we just kept going until 6:15.

Due to uncooperative markers/whiteboard, most Pax just made up scores, and YHC decreed Bowser defeated.

* Your Wife is not Your Best Friend; She is made for a much higher purpose.
* Joy Trumps Happiness. Happiness is a transitory positive feeling governed by mere external circumstance.

4 HIM initially came out to say Caw at their inner Jesters with a Poe-themed BD, joined by a fifth HIM for a caffeinated discussion.

Our Jester isn't just a persistent little bugger, he's crafty too. He knows that by trying to make us think it's all in our heads, that we're probably the only one struggling with this issue, that it's not actually that big of a deal and we can overcome it on our own, we won't open up and let other guys know about it.

That's a bald-faced lie.

We need to be open and honest about the challenges we're facing in our own lives. Not necessarily to everyone present at a CoT, not even to an F3 HIM specifically, but some other guy in our Concentrica whom we can trust. 

What stays in the shadows of our hearts and minds grows and strengthens, but when we bring it into the light with other guys, it is us who grow and are strengthened. 

Don't ever be afraid of being judged for opening up about something, either in person, in a DM, in a text, whatever. You've got guys on here who have faced either the same or probably pretty similar struggles in the past.

Q source: Jester
This week’s Q-source is about the daily discipline of being prepared to deal with one’s own jester. The jester is the temptations that a man faces which seek to hinder the improvement of the circumstances in the lives of those around him as well as improvement in his own life - his attempts to get right. Everyone has a jester, and the jester never leaves. If it seems like he has left, he is only waiting for a more opportune moment. Just as Cain was warned that “sin is crouching at the door and its desire is to be master over you,” so too we must always be vigilant and on guard against the jester. His main tools are various lies that attack our source of value and identity, make us think we have control when we really need help, convince us of moral relativism or moral licensing, or that life is found with the jester. But death, not life, is found with the jester, and the way to combat lies is with truth. 
One of the things that stuck out to me the most was the discussion about the lies told by our jester to keep us tied up, and that made me think of the following questions to reflect on: what areas of our lives do we allow lies to filter into? Or what lies are we feeding to others (knowingly or unknowingly) through our words and actions? What truth needs to be spoken in place of those lies for the benefit of those around us and for ourselves?

Fitness highs and fitness lows and which requires more discipline. 
The truth is that to Get Right we have to exert daily discipline over what we put in mouth no matter how fast we am Accelerating my King. Qsource  Queen

The Queen is an integral Guardrail in the HIM’s pursuit of proper personal alignment. As with chess, if the Queen is taken off the board, it is not long before the King finds himself checkmated. No matter how hard and consistently a man may exercise, if his diet is haphazard his Fitness kingdom will not long stand. The Queen cannot be ignored, even by the strongest of Kings.

The truth is that to Get Right I have to exert daily discipline over what I put in mouth no matter how fast I am Accelerating my King. In fact, it is in those periods of Acceleration that I have to be more disciplined in my service to the Queen. The reason is simple: more exercise means more calorie burn and more calorie burn means more hunger. The harder I exercise, the hungrier I get–the hungrier I get, the more I eat. That is the reason I can’t out-King my Queen. The faster I go on the Fitness road the higher my Guardrail needs to be to keep out of the ditch.

The Daily Discipline Of Physically Training The Body 
A man’s Right relationship with himself–his Fitness–begins with his body
Today's Q source emphasizes the importance of physical fitness for personal growth and preparedness. A man’s fitness is crucial because his body is the foundation for his soul and overall well-being. Fitness is not just about maintaining shape but continually improving speed, strength, stamina, and toughness to be prepared for life's challenges. The focus is on gradual, consistent improvement rather than staying static.
It talks about the concept of the "Royalty Race" which involves daily discipline in exercise (the King) and nutrition (the Queen), with the "Jester" representing distractions that can hinder progress. A man’s fitness should serve a greater purpose, building a kingdom of preparedness to protect and support others, not just for personal vanity.
Fitness should be accelerated through group support, where men challenge each other to push beyond their limits. Finally, the "Shield Lock" emphasizes collaboration, where men help each other grow stronger and achieve more than they could alone. Ultimately, a man should seek to surround himself with others who push him to improve and grow.

F3 the King is our fitness. Queen is our consumption. Put them together and you have a Kingdom. In order to have the Kingdom you want, you need to take care of both King and Queen.

The goal of the King is to constantly increase 3S2T: Speed, Strength, Stamina, Toughness (physical) and Toughness (mental). These are the aspects of a HIM’s physical kingdom that enable him to do the things he must do to be a Leader. It’s not really very complicated, how can a man be much of Leader if he gets smoked pulling his family’s luggage off the baggage carousel and carrying it to the minivan? Focused on mere survival, the Sad Clown zombie-shuffles through the motions of his life governed by his perception of what is expected of him from the world rather than in the manner for which he was created.

The Red forces a man to hike up the rocky path toward the EQV, while the Blue lets him mosey down the smooth trail to Mascot-life and chronic Sad Clown Syndrome. Some men have been adrift for so long that they resign themselves to being carried by life’s currents, focusing only on survival rather than progress. These men, known as Sad Clowns, suffer from a subtle but pervasive affliction—Sad Clown Syndrome—marked by physical weakness, loneliness, and a lack of purpose. Though they may appear content, their smiles mask a life spent merely going through the motions, dictated by external expectations rather than inner conviction. Without intervention, they remain stuck, unable to break free from their stagnant existence and make meaningful changes.

For transformation to occur, a man must commit to real change, shifting from the superficial efforts of an Amateur to the disciplined practice of a Pro. The Pro understands that true growth requires daily effort and preparation, not just the appearance of improvement. Like a professional athlete who trains beyond what is seen, the Pro commits to the unseen work of aligning his life with purpose. In contrast, the Amateur focuses on looking the part but crumbles when faced with challenges.

The path to personal alignment is steep, requiring constant effort in fitness, relationships, and faith, but it leads to true fulfillment. No man is too far gone to turn his life around; the journey begins with a single decisive step. By rejecting the comfortable illusion of progress and embracing real discipline, he chooses the difficult but rewarding path of becoming a High Impact Man (HIM). Over time, he builds routines that eliminate the need for constant decision-making, freeing him to act with conviction rather than hesitation.

Ultimately, discretion without discipline is a cage disguised as freedom—it leads to stagnation. True freedom comes from establishing strong guardrails that guide a man’s actions without reliance on fleeting motivation. The stronger the guardrails, the faster he can move forward, unburdened by the need to constantly decide whether to do what he already knows is necessary.

2nd Base: Carolina Dry Dock + Plank Jack

- Base Hit (ball over tennis net and no one catches it in air = Fielders do 2 Burpees
- Homerun (ball out of tennis court) = Fielders to 5 burpees.

Team 2 is in the “field” (opposite side of tennis court from batter) and does Side Straddle Hops AMRAP until ball is in play.

Thang 1: 4 Corners
Workout sheets were placed at each corner of the basketball court, except for one that was over by the benches. PAX numbered off 1-4, and divided out to the four corners.

Pick 1 exercise from the sheet and perform it, then move counterclockwise (or widdershins if you like fun words) around the basketball court to the next corner.

Mode of transport: 
Heel elevated lunges along the baseline (aka sneaky lunges)
Side shuffle along the sideline, pivot at half court

Do the exercises in any order you want. Repeat as time allows for 30 min.

Corner 1: Balance and foot stability
Foot plank left/Foot plank right 30 count each side

QSource - The Ted Lasso show had so many great messages and lessons from being authentic, believing in yourself, working as a team, to not not caring. At the same time, while the main character helped so many people he was not acknowledging the stresses in his life or asking for help, which ultimately led to his panic attacks. It is through those cracks we learn to realize we can’t manage all the challenges in this life all on our own power, and must rely on a greater power. God will provide and one way I’ve seen him provide is by putting these brothers in gloom in my life and knowing I have them there to support me. 1. Does a man’s need to be prepared change over time?
   - Yes. What a man goes through in life is what drives them to be prepared to handle again in the future. It can also change based on what their goals are and what they need to do to get there. Just because your goal changes though, does not mean you dump what you’ve gone through.

2. Is preparedness a mindset or a process?
   - I would say that it is a mindset that creates a process. Having a process does not create a mindset. Being prepared is a domino effect to get you to your process to handle your challenges in everyday life.

3. What drives a man’s desire to be prepared?
   - To not fall short and learn from one’s mistakes. A lot is on our shoulders that we have to bear. Luckily, you are not alone. You have your brothers in the Gloom to help.

The one and only Thang:
Run, ruck, carry
PAX split into teams of 2. We had 3 teams, which was perfect. Perform each of the following exercises with your Battle Buddy:

Run two full loops around the park. Keep your pace low enough to have a conversation with your Battle Buddy, which should keep you in Zone 2 or 3.

Pick up a ruck (weights available in 25#, 30#, 40#, 60#, and 80#) and ruck a full loop around the park. Try to maintain a 15-16 minute/mile pace. This should push your heart rate higher.

PAX 1 Farmer carries 2 cindies from the park sign to the pergola near the tennis courts while PAX 2 walks with him. PAX 2 Farmer carries the cindies back. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds there-and-back. This should bring your heart rate up, and then immediately back down. Also good for your grip strength and forearms!

Repeat as many circuits as possible in 30 minutes.

Q source: The LDP has four steps: schooling, apprenticeship, opportunity and failure. 
– First there is some kind of Schooling , the didactic instruction that the potential Leader receives on the timeless fundamentals of leadership.

– The second component is Apprenticeship , where the new Leader is given the chance to develop the skills he learned from his Schooling under the watchful eye of a more experienced Leader.

– Third comes Opportunity , the chance for the growing Leader to put what he has learned into practice under conditions where he is directly responsible for the outcome. While Schooling + Apprenticeship creates a Leader with the potential to be Effective, Opportunity is the required element for the man’s skill to become kinetic and have actual impact on his Group.

– The fourth component is Failure . A Lizard uses its LDP to intentionally court minor disaster in order to fully develop its Leaders, because it is from Failure that Leaders learn the most. Success teaches far less because it does not isolate what works from what does not the way Failure does.

The LDP depends upon decentralized execution to a central purpose. We do not dictate the precise manner in which our Leaders are to execute F3’s LDP but rather encourage and focus them upon our central purpose.

Q-source: Leadership Development Process (LDP)
Leaders are in short supply in most groups, but those groups which are led by great leaders won’t lack new leaders. Great leaders recognize that their time in any group is ultimately temporary. So, great leaders are constantly working themselves out of a job to ensure that the group will have leaders ready who will continue to seek the group’s advantage after they are gone, and this is done through the LDP. The LDP is tailored for the needs of each group, but every group’s LDP contains the same 4 basic components: schooling, apprenticeship, opportunity, and failure. The great leader teaches the new leader, then lets them practice, then gives them responsibility, and then “intentionally courts minor disaster” to help the new leader walk through failure. The last step, failure, helps isolate what works from what doesn’t in a way that is unique from the prior steps, and great leaders must know how to accept responsibility in failure rather than passing blame to others.

@Freedom proceeded to light fires inside Shipleys and fellowshipping was had while warm, melt in your mouth donuts were devoured. We said goodbye to our @Southie brothers to prepare for….

Q SOURCE

Man is naturally a group-forming creature, combining with others to achieve a mutual advantage that life alone cannot provide. A group is simply two or more people who voluntarily unite, whether for proximity, purpose, or a specific mission. This basic human drive to form groups is rooted in the inherent danger and impracticality of isolation, as vividly illustrated in Castaway with Chuck’s desperate need for companionship—even imagining it in a volleyball.

The three types of groups—communities, organizations, and teams—each serve unique roles. Communities form based on proximity, offering safety and harmony. Organizations unite people around a shared mission, with varying degrees of effectiveness, from forward-moving Lizards to stagnant Bullfrogs and purposeless Leeches. Teams, meanwhile, are purpose-driven units in close proximity, existing to solve problems for the benefit of a community, organization, or both.

Each type of group relies on leadership, but the method of leadership differs with the group type. Communities require leaders who enhance peace and harmony, organizations thrive under disruptive leaders who drive effectiveness, and teams demand active contributions and dynamic teamwork. Strong leadership across all three fosters healthy groups that can move toward advantage—a superior condition through purposeful action.

Ultimately, leadership is about guiding movement to advantage, and the QSource offers a framework to develop the skills needed to lead effectively in communities, organizations, and teams.

“The QSource is not a revolutionary theory of leadership. Revolutionary leadership theories are a myth because all leadership is founded upon a common set of principles that have been gradually evolving through trial and error since the first caveman led his tribe to higher ground to escape the rising flood waters.
What distinguishes one leadership philosophy from another- what makes it useful in a leader’s quest to influence movement to advantage-is it manner of organization and uniqueness in language.”
 
Quote from Socrates about language “The misuse of language induces evil in the soul”
 
Think about your language as a leader and the impact every word spoken has on those around you. To be the best leader you must choose your words with great precision. THE CLEAVER


Six F3 Aggieland HIMs took to the road this past Friday afternoon to head down to F3 Fort Bend’s The Shadows AO’s 1st anniversary 1st annual CSAUP event - The Cleaver. A 12hr overnight endurance event consisting of running, rucking and sandbag carrying in a battle buddy format (2 team members on course at a time); accumulating points per lap in an all out battle for total points accumulated at the end of 12 hours.

Points were per person, per lap
Each pax could choose how they wanted to complete the lap. Any combination was acceptable: ex - 1 slick, 1 ruck.

3.4 mile loop (in the shape of a cleaver)
Slick - 2pts
Ruck - 3pts
Ruck & sandbag - 4pts

We were the first to arrive at The Shadows AO and based off the course information provided we discussed the ideal location to set up our base camp. With the intention of being set up off to the side and out of the way of the main start stop area little did we know we had set up directly in front of it, arguably the best camp spot in the parking lot. F3 Aggieland sign and Forest Flag planted our site consisted of two canopies, two camping tables, chairs for each member, enough foam rollers to open a physical therapy club and even a green turf rug for comfort, stretching, and foam rolling; coolers and food, we were all set! 

Disclaimer given.

1st Thang: Tie Breaker

CIRCLE OF TRUST/BOM: Words shared at The Bomb Shelter AO by F3 Hammy 2018:

What does this time of year bring to your mind?  Past gatherings with family and friends? Reminders of favorite gifts received when you were young?  The excitement you had when you saw your wife or children open a special gift you gave them?  I certainly have those memories.

There is another memory I have and it comes to me every time I hear or sing Silent Night.  Back in the late ’60s and early ’70s, Bob Hope would take a USO show to the soldiers in Vietnam.  It was his way of bringing joy to a desperate place; his way of giving back to those who were giving so much for us back home. It was about two hours of comedy, song and dance, and beautiful women for the GIs to enjoy.  And did they ever enjoy the time.  The looks on their faces told it all.

As tradition had it, Bob Hope ended each show with clips from the several locations they visited.  That clip was a montage of the singing of Silent Night.  It was hard to keep the tears from flowing – from me or from the military personnel in the audiences.  It is a scene I will never forget.

All of this reminds me of the verse in Luke that captures the feelings of Mary on that first night of Jesus as a baby.  The shepherds had appeared at the manger and told Mary and Joseph all that the angels had told them about the child.  Luke 2:19 “But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.”

We need to do the same. We need to ponder the beauty of God’s gift of His Son.  The gift that is our only way to everlasting life with God.  And if we haven’t done a good enough job of it, we need to provide those experiences with the ones we love so they can treasure up and ponder for years to come.

Q Source-Leadership

Leadership is not an innate attribute like blue eyes or a square jaw but a skill that must be learned and mastered over time, much like playing the piano.

Becoming an effective leader requires a commitment to learning and practice; natural ability helps, but dedication is the key to mastery.

Even a man with limited natural talent can become a strong leader through consistent practice, while someone who refuses to practice will never reach their potential, no matter their innate qualities.

Leadership is a choice—no one can make it for you, and mastering it is a personal, deliberate, conscious decision.

F3, founded on January 1, 2011, began as a way for men to improve their lives through fitness but quickly recognized the need to strengthen leadership skills for families, workplaces, and communities.

To address this need, F3 developed leadership practices inspired by timeless principles, initially shared informally and later organized into a cohesive system.

From these efforts, the QSource emerged—a leadership manual rooted in enduring principles, designed to help men enhance their leadership skills and serve their communities effectively, wherever they may be.

Q-Source: Team Missionality (Q4.9) - https://f3nation.com/missionality-team
 The first step of Missionality is to determine the Problem the Team exists to solve or the Advantage it is seeking on behalf of the larger Group. This provides the Q with the Team’s Purpose. A Team can be formed for any legitimate Purpose, but it cannot exist simply to exist. In other words, if a Team’s Purpose includes the verb to be, than you have a Club not a Team.

For example:
• F3’s Problem to be solved is dormant Male Community Leadership
• F3’s Purpose (and the Advantage it seeks) is to invigorate Male Community Leadership
The second step of Missionality is to determine the means by which the Team will solve the Problem or seek the Advantage. This provides the Q with the Team’s Task, the thing that will be done to realize the Purpose.
• F3’s Task is to Plant, Serve and Grow men’s small Workout Groups
The third step of Missionality is to combine the Task and the Purpose into a short and concise statement of the Team’s Mission.
• F3’s Mission is to Plant, Serve and Grow men’s small Workout Groups in order to invigorate Male Community Leadership
The fourth step of Missionality is to write the Mission down someplace public so that the Members can read it, and to periodically ask them to recite it without reading it.
The fifth step of Missionality is to direct substantially all of the Team’s efforts and resources into the accomplishment of the Mission and resist all external pressure to do anything but that.
The Mission provides the Team with both direction (internally) and protection (externally). But it only works if the Q injects a spirit of Missionality into the Members by ensuring that Mission accomplishment is always the Team’s first priority.

Prioritizing Team Mission Accomplishment
Teamwork begins and ends with Mission

A HIM, because he is a Virtuous Leader, forms and deploys his Team to perform a specific Mission for the benefit of his Community or an Organization in which he is a Member. The Mission arises from an Advantage sought for the larger Group or in response to a Problem that the Community or Organization cannot itself remedy because it lacks the combination of Proximity and Purposefulness that is the distinguishing feature of the Team from other Groups. Communities cannot solve Problems (without Teams) because they are not Purposeful. Organizations, while Purposeful, also struggle to solve Problems (without Teams) because they lack the Proximity that is required to facilitate Teamwork, and without Teamwork, nothing of Advantage will happen.


A Team’s Mission is similar to a man’s Mission in that it is a Course Of Action taken to achieve a particular Purpose. A Course of Action is an integrated scheme of Tasks and Events that the Q devises to bring the Solution into fruition and eliminate a Problem or to gain Advantage for the larger Group. The Course of Action is the Team’s Mission, the things it does (its Tasks) and the reason it does them (it’s Articulated Purpose).


Tasks are different than Events. Whereas a Task is an action performed, an Event is something that occurs, whether planned or not. In Mutual Competence (Q3.2), we used the following example to illustrate the difference between Tasks and Events: baking a wedding cake is a Task, while the wedding reception is an Event. In the performance of the Team’s Mission, its Members will combine their actions through Tasks and Events in an efficient and potent way so that the Course of Action is successful.


Anything that distracts from the Mission inhibits Teamwork and is an enemy of Team Prosperity. Thus, the Q must constantly reinforce the Mission to focus the Team’s energy on achieving its Articulated Purpose and defend its Members from the temptation to expend resources on Problems that it was not formed to solve or Advantages that do not increase the Prosperity of the Community or Organization that the Team serves. Lack of focus and wasted energy are both distractions that the Q seeks to eliminate by prioritizing Team Mission Accomplishment.
The Team’s Mission is both directive and protective
The degree to which a Team is Dynamic will be based wholly upon its ability to accomplish its Mission. Teams that can’t or won’t perform their Mission become static and ultimately morph into Clubs or simply disintegrate.
To keep that from happening, the Q constantly reinforces Missionality by ensuring that Mission accomplishment is the Team’s first priority. This requires Deliberatude, for the Q will encounter both the internal tendency of the Members to coast or become distracted by shiny non-Missional objects, and external demands that have nothing to do with the Mission.


It is easy to determine if the Q is reinforcing Missionality within his Team. Simply ask a Member to tell you what the Mission is. If he can’t do that, ask him what the Team does, and why the Team does it. If he can’t answer either of those questions, the Q is not reinforcing Team Missionality.

F3’s Purpose (and the Advantage it seeks) is to invigorate Male Community Leadership
The second step of Missionality is to determine the means by which the Team will solve the Problem or seek the Advantage. This provides the Q with the Team’s Task, the thing that will be done to realize the Purpose.


F3’s Task is to Plant, Serve and Grow men’s small Workout Groups


The third step of Missionality is to combine the Task and the Purpose into a short and concise statement of the Team’s Mission.


F3’s Mission is to Plant, Serve and Grow men’s small Workout Groups in order to invigorate Male Community Leadership


The fourth step of Missionality is to write the Mission down someplace public so that the Members can read it, and to periodically ask them to recite it without reading it.


The fifth step of Missionality is to direct substantially all of the Team’s efforts and resources into the accomplishment of the Mission and resist all external pressure to do anything but that.


The Mission provides the Team with both direction (internally) and protection (externally). But it only works if the Q injects a spirit of Missionality into the Members by ensuring that Mission accomplishment is always the Team’s first priority.
With Missionality, a sidewind is the same as a headwind
I stepped up to the tee of a par 3 one blustery day and did what I’d seen good golfers do for years–I threw some grass in the air to gauge the wind direction. Sweeper Boy asked me why I was doing that.


“Well, you know (wondering why a guy who was a much better golfer than me was asking me that), so I know how to handle the wind.” I replied uncertainly.


“I get that,” he said, “but what difference does the wind on the tee box make? Just look at the flag and see if the wind on the green is at your back.”


“OK, but what if it’s a sidewind?” I asked, a little confused.


“Same as a headwind: hit an extra club. If there’s wind, it’s either at your back or not. Sidewind is the same as headwind.” Sweeper was right about that. In golf, the wind is either directly helping or it’s hurting. No wind is neutral–a sidewind is the same as a headwind. The same is true with Teamwork. Every action a Team Member takes is either directly in furtherance of the Mission or it is inhibiting Mission accomplishment. There is no such thing as a sidewind when it comes to Teamwork.


Take the NFL as an example. The Purpose of the NFL (which is an Organization) is to make money. It’s publicly stated Purpose might be something more Gooistic, but that’s just public relations. As a Group, it exists to make money, as much money as possible. As a football fan and a capitalist, I have absolutely no problem with that.


To achieve its Purpose of making money, the NFL performs a particular Task, which is to pit its 32 Teams against one another in weekly football games in order to entertain its stadium and television audiences, from whom it collects revenue in a variety of very inventive ways. The Teams (I’m talking about the players and coaches), while they are part of an Organization formed to make money, actually have a different Purpose and that is to win football games. They get paid to coach and play, but their Purpose is to win. If they don’t win, they will shortly find themselves making much less money.


Collectively, the NFL can never “win” more than 256 games in any given football season. That’s because it has 32 Teams who play 16 games each (I’m taking out ties to keep the point simple). Thus, it is cannot logically be the NFL’s Purpose to win football games, because it will always win the same number of games no matter what it does. But the Teams? They have to win, or their coaches will get fired and their players cut. Their Purpose is clearly to win games. Making money is downstream from winning for them.


Although the NFL and its Teams have different Purposes, they align and support one another very well. When the players practice hard to gain the Advantage they need to win, the games are better played and the audience is more entertained. That leads to more money for the NFL and more money for the players. That is a very effective Incentive. Thus, practicing hard and playing well are clearly tailwinds for both the Teams and the NFL, in that they are activities that advance the Prosperity of both.


Conversely, If the players say and do things that are appealing to the NFL’s fans, that doesn’t impact the outcome of the games or make them more entertaining, although it probably has some indirect impact on making money in the sense that happier fans are stickier fans. Thus, having the players say and do appealing things are mild tailwinds for the NFL but not for the Teams. For the Teams, they are sidewinds–the question being how strong.


However, if the players say or doing controversial things (rather than appealing things) during the games, things that might please a portion of the audience but will aggravate, anger or distance another sizable portion of the audience, that’s a different story. If it reduces the size of the audience and/or their willingness to purchase its licensed products, that is clearly a headwind to the NFL because it reduces its revenue.


But what is it to the Teams? Just like the saying and doing of appealing things, controversial things is not a headwind because it does not reduce winning. But it does not increase winning either, so it is at best a sidewind, and when it comes to Teamwork a sidewind is the same as a headwind. It doesn’t advance the Mission. In golf, it requires more club to hit the ball the same distance. With Teams, it saps resources the Team needs to accomplish its Mission and obscures the focus of the Team Members. It makes the Team less Prosperous.


By now, you’ve probably determined that I’m referring obliquely to the Anthem Protest that began with Colin Kaepernick in 2016. Reasonable minds can differ as to whether the Anthem Protest is a “good” thing or not (I’m not taking a position either way), but I doubt there would be much argument over whether it is a controversial thing. A large percentage of fans support it, but a (roughly) equal percentage oppose it, and the feelings of both factions run high.


While there there is certainly an argument to be made that the Anthem Protest arises from a very important societal issue and that an exception to the sidewind rule should be made, the challenge for the Leaders of the Teams is that in doing so they might open the door for other important societal issues. Once you’ve allowed resources to be diverted from the Team’s Purpose for one important thing, there is no real argument against doing it again, and again and again.


One could also reasonably argue that it is the NFL itself that first opened this door when it began playing the national anthem prior to its games. So, this argument would go, if playing the anthem is an acceptable sidewind, who is to say that protesting the anthem is not also acceptable? That’s a pretty good argument, and it has created a Problem that the NFL and its Teams have to solve.


I am not proposing a Solution to the Problem, but I am contending that the Leaders of the NFL and its Teams have not done so either. They have allowed this sidewind to blow for two years (at the time of this writing) hoping, apparently, the storm will subside on its own. I further contend that it is not Effective Leadership to allow an Iceberg of a Problem fester in hopes that it will melt away on its own. Either the NFL and its Teams should embrace the Anthem Protest as an acceptable sidewind (in the same way they embraced the anthem itself), or take action to stop it. There is no middle path.


If a Leader does not prioritize Team Mission accomplishment it is very unlikely that its Mission will be accomplished.

The MOG Mile: 
4 Rounds of:
* 19 Cindy ground-to-overhead
* 19 Cindy front squats
* 19 Cindy merkins (ea. hand = 38 total)
* 400 meter Cindy carry

Background & Significance: 
This hero workout is dedicated to the members of the 3rd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment, and 1st SFOD-D (Delta Force), supported by pilots from the 160th Aviation Regiment (Nightstalkers) and other SF units, who went into the city of Mogadishu, Somalia to execute Operation ‘Gothic Serpent’, an attempt to apprehend key players in Mohammed Farrah Aidid’s dictatorship on October 3, 1993.

While the initial mission went smoothly, things took a turn for the worse when two aircraft were shot down, forever coining the phrase ‘Blackhawk Down’. Determined to not leave a man behind, and also facing the task of securing the crash sites, Rangers and Deltas, scattered at several locations throughout the city, under heavy fire, most of them wounded, and low on supplies, held their positions until the morning hours of October 4th.

As help from the 10th Mountain Division finally arrived, the armored vehicles could not accommodate all of the soldiers. At this point, some of them began their exit to a rallying point on foot, under heavy fire, dehydrated and sleep-deprived, all of them wounded in one way or another. This has become known as the “Mogadishu Mile.”

You cover a total distance of one mile. Even though the soldiers actually walked between 2.5 and 3 miles depending on their starting point, it has become known as a “mile”. 

You carry your cindy during the run to symbolize the gear the soldiers carried.

– 19 reps one honoring each soldier of Task Force Ranger killed during the battle and the day after.

– Ground-to-Overheads as the soldiers held up their rifles the entire time

– Squats as they sought cover behind anything available

– Push-Ups (Merkins) as they fell to the ground and had to get back up

– Don’t let cindy go – symbolic of the dedication the soldiers showed towards their creed to “not leave a man behind.”

The concept is simple, each round you determine how many reps of each exercise you do. The only catch is that all 3 exercises have to add up to 100.
